blocks.explain: Enumerate both structural models exactly, confirm the identical observational table, compute the interventional answers, show that the naive contrast estimates $0.6$ whichever model produced the data, and evaluate the bounds of the next section.
blocks.source:
import itertools
import numpy as np

def bern(p, v):
    return p if v == 1 else 1 - p

def m1(do_x=None):        # U ~ Bern(1/2), X := U xor N_X (0.1), Y := U xor N_Y (0.125)
    P = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for u, nx, ny in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=3):
        x = (u ^ nx) if do_x is None else do_x
        P[x, u ^ ny] += 0.5 * bern(0.1, nx) * bern(0.125, ny)
    return P

def m2(do_x=None):        # X ~ Bern(1/2), Y := X xor N_Y (0.2)
    P = np.zeros((2, 2))
    for x0, ny in itertools.product((0, 1), repeat=2):
        x = x0 if do_x is None else do_x
        P[x, x ^ ny] += 0.5 * bern(0.2, ny)
    return P

print("observational P(X, Y), M1:\n", m1(), "\nM2:\n", m2(), "\nequal:", np.allclose(m1(), m2()))
for name, m in (("M1", m1), ("M2", m2)):
    ate = m(1)[1, 1] - m(0)[0, 1]
    print(f"{name}: P(Y=1|do(X=1)) = {m(1)[1, 1]:.2f},  ATE = {ate:.2f}")

# any estimator sees the same data law: the naive contrast converges to 0.6 under BOTH models
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
P = m1().ravel()
draws = rng.choice(4, size=20000, p=P)          # identical draws would come from M2
x, y = draws // 2, draws % 2
print("naive contrast from 20000 samples:", round(y[x == 1].mean() - y[x == 0].mean(), 3), "(true ATE: 0 in M1, 0.6 in M2)")

def ate_bounds(gamma, px1=0.5, p1=0.8, p0=0.2):
    """Sharp bounds when |P(Y_x=1|X=1-x) - P(Y_x=1|X=x)| <= gamma; gamma = 1 gives the no-assumption bounds."""
    px0 = 1 - px1
    e1 = (px1 * p1 + px0 * max(0, p1 - gamma), px1 * p1 + px0 * min(1, p1 + gamma))
    e0 = (px0 * p0 + px1 * max(0, p0 - gamma), px0 * p0 + px1 * min(1, p0 + gamma))
    return round(e1[0] - e0[1], 10), round(e1[1] - e0[0], 10)

for g in (0, 0.2, 0.6, 0.8, 1):
    print(f"gamma = {g}: ATE in {ate_bounds(g)}")

sections.heading: Partial identification: what the data do pin down

blocks.md: Non-identified does not mean uninformative. Write $Y_x$ for the potential outcome under $\mathrm{do}(X = x)$, with **consistency**: if $X = x$ then $Y_x = Y$. Splitting on the observed treatment,

blocks.title: No-assumption bounds
blocks.label: prop-l7-05-bounds
blocks.md:
For binary $X, Y$ and any model consistent with $P(X, Y)$,

$$P(x_1, y_1) \le P(Y_1{=}1) \le P(x_1, y_1) + P(x_0), \qquad P(x_0, y_1) \le P(Y_0{=}1) \le P(x_0, y_1) + P(x_1),$$

and the resulting interval for the ATE has width exactly 1. The bounds are sharp. These are the no-assumption (natural) bounds of Manski (1990). For our table, $P(Y_1{=}1) \in [0.4, 0.9]$, $P(Y_0{=}1) \in [0.1, 0.6]$, and $\text{ATE} \in [-0.2, 0.8]$.

The bounds follow from [](#eq-l7-05-split) and its analog for $Y_0$. The ATE interval is $[P(x_1,y_1) - P(x_0,y_1) - P(x_1),\ P(x_1,y_1) + P(x_0) - P(x_0,y_1)]$, of width $P(x_0) + P(x_1) = 1$. For sharpness, build a model on $(X, Y_0, Y_1)$ with the observed $P(X)$ and $P(Y_x{=}1 \mid X{=}x)$, and choose $P(Y_1{=}1 \mid X{=}0)$ and $P(Y_0{=}1 \mid X{=}1)$ freely in $[0, 1]$ with $Y_0, Y_1$ independent given $X$. Every such choice reproduces $P(X, Y)$ by consistency, and the extreme choices attain the endpoints.

blocks.alt: A derivation that turns into the interval from -0.2 to 0.8 on a number line with M1 at 0 and M2 at 0.6, then a sweep that shrinks the interval to the single point 0.6.
blocks.caption: Consistency plus the unseen term between 0 and $P(X = 0)$ gives $\text{ATE} \in [-0.2, 0.8]$. Bounding confounding by $\gamma$ shrinks the set; M1 leaves it once $\gamma < 0.6$.
blocks.describe: The equation $P(Y_1 = 1) = P(Y_1 = 1, X = 1) + P(Y_1 = 1, X = 0)$ appears. By consistency the first term becomes the observed $P(Y = 1, X = 1) = 0.4$; the unseen second term lies between 0 and $P(X = 0) = 0.5$, so $P(Y_1 = 1) \in [0.4, 0.9]$. Likewise $P(Y_0 = 1) \in [0.1, 0.6]$, and the ATE lies in $[0.4 - 0.6, 0.9 - 0.1] = [-0.2, 0.8]$. A violet bar covers that interval on a number line; a red dot marks M1 at 0 and a cyan dot marks M2 at 0.6, both inside. Then the assumption that confounding shifts $P(Y_x = 1)$ between treatment groups by at most $\gamma$ is written, and $\gamma$ decreases from 1. The bar shrinks from both ends; at $\gamma = 0.6$ its left end reaches 0, where M1 sits, so explaining the effect away needs confounding of at least 0.6. At $\gamma = 0$ the bar is the single point 0.6.

blocks.title: Sensitivity bounds
blocks.label: prop-l7-05-sens
blocks.md:
Assume $|P(Y_x{=}1 \mid X{=}1{-}x) - P(Y_x{=}1 \mid X{=}x)| \le \gamma$ for $x \in \{0, 1\}$. With $p_1 = P(y_1 \mid x_1)$ and $p_0 = P(y_1 \mid x_0)$, the sharp bounds are

$$P(Y_1{=}1) \in P(x_1)p_1 + P(x_0)\big[\max(0, p_1 - \gamma),\ \min(1, p_1 + \gamma)\big],$$

and symmetrically for $P(Y_0{=}1)$. For our table the ATE lies in $[\max(0.6 - \gamma, -0.2),\ \min(0.6 + \gamma, 0.8)]$. The value $0$ is inside exactly when $\gamma \ge 0.6$, and M1 has confounding $\gamma = 0.6$: $P(Y_1{=}1 \mid X{=}1) - P(Y_1{=}1 \mid X{=}0) = 0.8 - 0.2$.

blocks.caption: Slide the confounding bound $\gamma$. The identified set for the ATE (left) and its endpoints as functions of $\gamma$ (right). At $\gamma = 0$ the effect is identified as $0.6$; at $\gamma = 1$ it is the no-assumption interval.
blocks.describe: The left panel shows the identified set for the average treatment effect as a violet bar on an axis from $-0.35$ to $0.95$, with diamonds for M1 at 0 and M2 at 0.6. The right panel plots the lower bound $\max(0.6 - \gamma, -0.2)$ and the upper bound $\min(0.6 + \gamma, 0.8)$ against $\gamma$ from 0 to 1, with the region between shaded and a dashed line at the chosen $\gamma$. At $\gamma = 0$ the set is the point 0.6. The upper bound reaches 0.8 at $\gamma = 0.2$; the lower bound reaches 0 at $\gamma = 0.6$ and $-0.2$ at $\gamma = 0.8$, after which the set stays $[-0.2, 0.8]$.

blocks.title: Three repairs, three different assumptions
blocks.md: **Intervene:** randomize $X$; the data map then contains $P(Y \mid \mathrm{do}(X))$ and the target is a function of it. **Measure more:** if $U$ is recorded and the graph of M1 is assumed, the backdoor formula $\sum_u P(y \mid x, u)P(u)$ identifies the effect (it gives $0.5$ for both $x$ in M1, with positivity since $P(x \mid u) \in \{0.1, 0.9\}$) [@pearlcausality]. **Narrow the class:** assume no confounding ($\gamma = 0$), which identifies $0.6$ but is an assumption the data cannot check. If none is available, report the interval.

sections.heading: A quantum pair: restricted measurements

blocks.title: Coherence hidden by the measurement basis
blocks.label: ex-l7-05-dephase
blocks.md: Let the data map be: prepare $|0\rangle$, send it through the unknown qubit channel, measure $Z$. The identity channel and complete $Z$ dephasing $\mathcal{Z}(\rho) = \tfrac12(\rho + Z\rho Z)$ both output $|0\rangle$ and give outcome 0 with probability 1. The target "coherence transmission", say $\langle X\rangle$ at the output for input $|+\rangle$, is 1 for the identity and 0 for $\mathcal{Z}$. By Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-noest) no amount of $Z$ data on $|0\rangle$ can estimate it. Adding the input $|+\rangle$ and an $X$ measurement separates them: outcome $+$ with probability 1 versus $1/2$.

blocks.title: Tomographically complete designs identify the channel
blocks.label: prop-l7-05-tomo
blocks.md: If the input states $\{\rho_k\}$ span the space of operators on the input and the output measurements are informationally complete, then $D(\mathcal{E}_1) = D(\mathcal{E}_2)$ implies $\mathcal{E}_1 = \mathcal{E}_2$. For a qubit, the inputs $|0\rangle, |1\rangle, |+\rangle, |{+i}\rangle$ and measurements of $X$, $Y$, $Z$ suffice.

Informational completeness means the measured statistics determine each output state $\mathcal{E}(\rho_k)$. A channel is linear, and the $\rho_k$ span the operator space, so its values on the $\rho_k$ determine it everywhere. For a qubit, $|0\rangle\langle0| \pm |1\rangle\langle1|$ give $I$ and $Z$, and $2|+\rangle\langle+| - I = X$, $2|{+i}\rangle\langle{+i}| - I = Y$ [@nielsenchuang].

blocks.title: The channel is identifiable; its dilation is not
blocks.md: Kraus operators $\{K_i\}$ and $\{\sum_j u_{ij}K_j\}$ with $u$ unitary define the same channel [@nielsenchuang]. Complete dephasing has both $\{I/\sqrt2, Z/\sqrt2\}$ and $\{|0\rangle\langle0|, |1\rangle\langle1|\}$. A target that depends on the decomposition, such as "which Kraus event happened", is therefore not identified by any input-output data, even tomographically complete data. This parallels classical counterfactuals, which interventional data alone do not fix ([L4-09](#lesson-l4-09)): such targets need additional model structure, stated as an assumption.

sections.heading: Quantum data can identify a causal direction

blocks.md: Two qubits $A$ and $B$ are measured in the same Pauli basis $\sigma_i \in \{X, Y, Z\}$, giving outcomes $a, b = \pm1$. Two model classes: a **common cause**, where $A$ and $B$ are halves of a shared state $\rho_{AB}$, so $c_i = \mathbb{E}[ab] = \operatorname{Tr}[\rho_{AB}\,\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_i]$; and a **direct cause** $A \to B$, where $A$ starts maximally mixed, is measured projectively, and its post-measurement eigenstate is sent through a channel $\mathcal{E}$ to $B$. Then $\Pr(a) = 1/2$, the state sent is $(I + a\sigma_i)/2$, and

With $Z$ measurements only, the identity channel, the classical common cause $\tfrac12(|00\rangle\langle00| + |11\rangle\langle11|)$ and the entangled common cause $|\Phi^+\rangle = (|00\rangle + |11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ all give $c_{zz} = 1$ and uniform marginals: classically, direction is not identified. Adding $X$ and $Y$ gives $(c_{xx}, c_{yy}, c_{zz}) = (1, 1, 1)$, $(0, 0, 1)$ and $(1, -1, 1)$. Since $\sum_i \sigma_i\otimes\sigma_i = 2F - I$ with $F$ the swap, every state has $c_{xx} + c_{yy} + c_{zz} = 2\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F) - 1 \le 1$, so the identity channel's sum of 3 cannot come from any common cause.

blocks.alt: Three columns of bars for an identity channel, a classical common cause and an entangled common cause; the Z bars are all +1, then X and Y bars differ, and their sums are 3, 1 and 1.
blocks.caption: In the $Z$ basis the three models agree. The $X$ and $Y$ correlations separate them, and $c_{xx} + c_{yy} + c_{zz} \le 1$ for every state rules out a common cause for the identity channel's pattern.
blocks.describe: Three columns are labeled: a direct cause $A \to B$ through the identity channel, a classical common cause, and a common cause in the state $|\Phi^+\rangle$. First a $c_{zz}$ bar appears in each column, all of height $+1$, with the note that measuring $Z$ on both sides makes all three look the same. Then $c_{xx}$ bars appear: $+1$, $0$, $+1$. Then $c_{yy}$ bars: $+1$, $0$, $-1$. The sums are 3, 1 and 1. The bound $c_{xx} + c_{yy} + c_{zz} \le 1$ for every state, because the sum equals $2\operatorname{Tr}(\rho F) - 1$, closes the scene.

blocks.md: The next theorem was proved in [L6-05](#lesson-l6-05). We restate it with a compact proof because the identification arguments below (the octahedron, the mixing-weight bound of the worked example) use its exact inequalities. Part (i) is the classical picture of Bell-diagonal states as a tetrahedron, whose separable members form the octahedron $|c_1| + |c_2| + |c_3| \le 1$ [@horodecki1996pra]; the use of the dual tetrahedron to infer causal direction from passive observation is the idea behind [@ried2015].

blocks.title: Two tetrahedra of correlation triples
blocks.label: thm-l7-05-tetra

blocks.md: (i) The Pauli twirl $\rho' = \tfrac14\sum_{k=0}^{3} (\sigma_k\otimes\sigma_k)\rho(\sigma_k\otimes\sigma_k)$, with $\sigma_0 = I$, is a state. Conjugation by $\sigma_k\otimes\sigma_k$ multiplies $\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_j$ by $s_k(i)s_k(j)$, where $s_k(i) = \pm1$ records whether $\sigma_k$ commutes with $\sigma_i$; the characters satisfy $\sum_k s_k(i)s_k(j) = 4\delta_{ij}$ for $i, j \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$. So the twirl keeps $\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_i$ and removes every other Pauli term: $\rho' = \tfrac14(I + \sum_i c_i\,\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_i)$ with the same $c$. Its eigenvectors are the Bell states, where $(XX, YY, ZZ)$ take the values $(1,-1,1)$ on $|\Phi^+\rangle$, $(-1,1,1)$ on $|\Phi^-\rangle$, $(1,1,-1)$ on $|\Psi^+\rangle$ and $(-1,-1,-1)$ on $|\Psi^-\rangle$, which gives the four eigenvalues $\tfrac14(1 + c_1 - c_2 + c_3)$ and so on. Positivity is the four inequalities. (ii) The twirled channel $\mathcal{E}'(\rho) = \tfrac14\sum_k \sigma_k\mathcal{E}(\sigma_k\rho\sigma_k)\sigma_k$ is a channel with the same $t$, it is unital, and by the same character sum $\mathcal{E}'(\sigma_i) = t_i\sigma_i$. Its Choi state $(\mathrm{id}\otimes\mathcal{E}')(|\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+|)$, starting from $|\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+| = \tfrac14(I + XX - YY + ZZ)$, equals $\tfrac14(I + t_1XX - t_2YY + t_3ZZ)$, a state with triple $(t_1, -t_2, t_3)$, so (i) applies. (iii) The vertices are the Bell states and the four Pauli unitary channels. The two systems of inequalities together are $\pm c_1 \pm c_2 \pm c_3 \le 1$ for all eight sign choices, which is the octahedron.

blocks.alt: A rotating cube containing a blue tetrahedron, an amber tetrahedron pointing the other way, and a violet octahedron where they overlap, with three marked points.
blocks.caption: The correlation triples of all common-cause states (blue) and of all direct causes (amber) form dual tetrahedra in the cube $[-1, 1]^3$. Inside the violet octahedron $|c_1| + |c_2| + |c_3| \le 1$ the direction is not identified.
blocks.describe: A wire cube spans $-1$ to $1$ on the axes $\langle XX\rangle$, $\langle YY\rangle$, $\langle ZZ\rangle$. A blue tetrahedron is drawn, with vertices at the four Bell-state triples; a key says it holds the correlations of any common-cause state. An amber tetrahedron follows, pointing the opposite way, with vertices at the triples of the four Pauli unitary channels; its key says any direct-cause channel $A \to B$. Their overlap, a violet octahedron, fades in with the formula $|c_1| + |c_2| + |c_3| \le 1$. Three points appear: the identity channel at $(1, 1, 1)$, a vertex of the amber tetrahedron outside the blue one; $|\Phi^+\rangle$ at $(1, -1, 1)$, a vertex of the blue tetrahedron outside the amber one; and the classical common cause at $(0, 0, 1)$, a vertex of the octahedron, compatible with both. The camera then circles the solids.

blocks.caption: Rotate the solids and move an observed triple along the diagonal $(s, s, s)$, from the singlet at $s = -1$ to the identity channel at $s = 1$. The title reports which model class can explain it.
blocks.describe: A 3-D view of the cube $[-1, 1]^3$ with the blue tetrahedron of common-cause states, the amber tetrahedron of direct-cause channels and the violet edges of their octahedral overlap. Labeled points mark $|\Phi^+\rangle$ at $(1, -1, 1)$, the identity channel at $(1, 1, 1)$, the classical common cause at $(0, 0, 1)$ and the singlet at $(-1, -1, -1)$. A red marker moves along $(s, s, s)$ as the slider goes from $-1$ to $1$ in steps of $0.2$: for $s \le -0.4$ only a common cause fits, for $-0.2 \le s \le 0.2$ both fit and the direction is not identified, and for $s \ge 0.4$ only a direct cause fits. The exact switch points are $s = \pm 1/3$.

blocks.explain: Compute the triples of the three models, then check Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-tetra) on 3000 random two-qubit states and 3000 random qubit channels (from random isometries).
blocks.source:
# Same-basis Pauli correlation triples: states versus channels
I2 = np.eye(2); X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1, -1])
P3 = (X, Y, Z)

def c_state(rho):                    # (<XX>, <YY>, <ZZ>) of a two-qubit state
    return np.array([np.real(np.trace(rho @ np.kron(s, s))) for s in P3])

def c_channel(kraus):                # t_i = (1/2) Tr[s_i E(s_i)]: A maximally mixed, measured in s_i, eigenstate sent through E
    return np.array([0.5 * np.real(np.trace(s @ sum(K @ s @ K.conj().T for K in kraus))) for s in P3])

phi = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1]) / np.sqrt(2)
models = {"identity channel": c_channel([I2]),
          "classical common cause": c_state(np.diag([0.5, 0, 0, 0.5])),
          "Phi+ common cause": c_state(np.outer(phi, phi))}
for k, v in models.items():
    print(f"{k:24s} c = {v.round(3)}   sum = {v.sum():+.0f}")

state_ok = lambda c: min(1 - c[0] - c[1] - c[2], 1 - c[0] + c[1] + c[2], 1 + c[0] - c[1] + c[2], 1 + c[0] + c[1] - c[2]) >= -1e-9
chan_ok = lambda t: min(1 + t[0] + t[1] + t[2], 1 + t[0] - t[1] - t[2], 1 - t[0] + t[1] - t[2], 1 - t[0] - t[1] + t[2]) >= -1e-9

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
def random_state():                  # random mixed two-qubit state (Ginibre)
    G = rng.normal(size=(4, 4)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(4, 4)); R = G @ G.conj().T
    return R / np.trace(R)

def random_channel():                # random qubit channel from a random isometry into qubit x environment
    G = rng.normal(size=(8, 2)) + 1j * rng.normal(size=(8, 2)); V, _ = np.linalg.qr(G)
    return [V[2 * k:2 * k + 2, :] for k in range(4)]   # Kraus operators, sum K^dag K = I

S = [c_state(random_state()) for _ in range(3000)]
C = [c_channel(random_channel()) for _ in range(3000)]
print("all states in their tetrahedron:", all(map(state_ok, S)), "| max sum over states:", round(max(s.sum() for s in S), 3))
print("all channels in their tetrahedron:", all(map(chan_ok, C)))
print("identity channel compatible with any state?", state_ok(models["identity channel"]))
print("classical common cause compatible with a channel?", chan_ok(models["classical common cause"]))

blocks.caption: Identification comes before architecture. A counterexample pair settles non-identification for that design; a proof is needed for identification.

blocks.title: Mixtures of mechanisms enlarge the class
blocks.md: Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-tetra) compares a pure common cause with a pure direct cause. If the true process can be a probabilistic or coherent mixture of both, the model class is larger and points outside the octahedron no longer pin down a single mechanism; one can still bound the weight of each, as the worked example shows. Ried et al. report an experiment in which quantum correlations alone sometimes resolve the causal question; read it to see which model class they assume [@ried2015]. Coherent mixtures need the process formalism of [L6-07](#lesson-l6-07).

worked_example.title: How much direct cause must there be?
worked_example.problem: A process is a probabilistic mixture: with probability $w$ a direct cause $A \to B$ through some channel, otherwise a common cause through some state. The observed triple is $c = (0.6, 0.6, 0.6)$. Find the smallest $w$ compatible with Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-tetra), and a decomposition attaining it.
steps: The observed triple is linear in the mixture: $c = w\,t + (1 - w)\,c'$ with $t$ in the channel tetrahedron and $c'$ in the state tetrahedron.
Sum the coordinates. States satisfy $c'_1 + c'_2 + c'_3 \le 1$ and channels $t_1 + t_2 + t_3 \le 3$. So $1.8 \le 3w + (1 - w) = 1 + 2w$, giving $w \ge 0.4$.

Attain it: take $t = (1, 1, 1)$ (identity channel) and $c' = (c - 0.4\,t)/0.6 = (1/3, 1/3, 1/3)$. Check $c'$: $1 - 3\cdot\tfrac13 = 0$ and $1 + \tfrac13 - \tfrac13 + \tfrac13 > 0$, so it is a valid state triple (a Bell-diagonal state on the boundary of the tetrahedron).
Hence the identified set for $w$ is $[0.4, 1]$: the upper end is attained by $w = 1$ with $t = c$, which lies in the channel tetrahedron since $1 + 3(0.6) > 0$ and $1 + 0.6 - 1.2 > 0$.
worked_example.result: The data identify not $w$ but the interval $[0.4, 1]$: at least 40 percent direct cause. A point claim about $w$ would need a further assumption or a further experiment, such as an intervention on $A$.

exercises.prompt: A learner trained on the $Z$-basis records of Example [](#ex-l7-05-dephase) reports the identity channel because of a minimum-noise prior. Is the coherence conclusion identified by the data? Specify an experiment that tests it.
exercises.solution: No. The identity and complete dephasing give the same data, so the conclusion comes from the prior (Remark on priors). Prepare $|+\rangle$, send it through the device, and measure $X$: the identity gives $+$ with probability 1, complete dephasing gives $+$ with probability $1/2$. A few dozen shots separate them with high confidence.

exercises.prompt: Compute the no-assumption ATE bounds for $P(X{=}1) = 0.3$, $P(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}1) = 0.9$, $P(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}0) = 0.5$.
Show that in M1 the backdoor formula with the recorded $U$ returns ATE $= 0$, and explain why it would fail if $N_X$ were absent ($X = U$).
exercises.solution: $P(Y{=}1 \mid x, u) = P(U \oplus N_Y = 1 \mid U = u) = 0.875$ if $u = 1$ and $0.125$ if $u = 0$, for either $x$. So $\sum_u P(y_1 \mid x, u)P(u) = \tfrac12(0.875 + 0.125) = 0.5$ for both $x$ and the ATE is 0. If $X = U$, then $P(X = 1 \mid U = 0) = 0$, so $P(y \mid x_1, u_0)$ is undefined: positivity fails and the backdoor formula cannot be evaluated, even though $U$ is observed.

exercises.prompt: Prove that complete dephasing has the two Kraus decompositions $\{I/\sqrt2, Z/\sqrt2\}$ and $\{|0\rangle\langle0|, |1\rangle\langle1|\}$, and give the unitary relating them.
exercises.solution: $\tfrac12(\rho + Z\rho Z)$ keeps the diagonal of $\rho$ and kills the off-diagonal, as does $|0\rangle\langle0|\rho|0\rangle\langle0| + |1\rangle\langle1|\rho|1\rangle\langle1|$. With $u = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$: $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(I/\sqrt2 + Z/\sqrt2) = (I + Z)/2 = |0\rangle\langle0|$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(I/\sqrt2 - Z/\sqrt2) = |1\rangle\langle1|$.

exercises.prompt: Prove the character identity $\sum_{k=0}^{3} s_k(i)s_k(j) = 4\delta_{ij}$ used in Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-tetra), where $\sigma_k\sigma_i\sigma_k = s_k(i)\sigma_i$.
exercises.solution: $s_k(0) = 1$ and $s_0(i) = 1$; for $i, k \ge 1$, $s_k(i) = 1$ if $k = i$ and $-1$ otherwise. If $i = j$ the sum is $\sum_k s_k(i)^2 = 4$. If $i = 0 \ne j$: $\sum_k s_k(j) = 1 + 1 - 1 - 1 = 0$. If $i, j \ge 1$ distinct: $k = 0$ gives $+1$, $k = i$ gives $s_i(j) = -1$, $k = j$ gives $-1$, and the third index gives $(-1)(-1) = +1$; total 0.

exercises.prompt: Under Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-tetra) a common cause yields $c_{xx} + c_{yy} + c_{zz} \le 1$. Find the largest value of the same sum for a direct cause, the channels attaining it, and the largest value of $c_{xx} - c_{yy} + c_{zz}$ for each class. Which combination best detects an entangled common cause?
exercises.solution: For channels $t_1 + t_2 + t_3 \le 3$, attained only by the identity channel (vertex $(1,1,1)$). For $c_1 - c_2 + c_3$: on the state tetrahedron the maximum over vertices is 3, at $|\Phi^+\rangle = (1, -1, 1)$; on the channel tetrahedron the vertices give $1, 1, -3, 1$, so the maximum is 1 (from the inequality $1 - t_1 + t_2 - t_3 \ge 0$). So $c_{xx} - c_{yy} + c_{zz} > 1$ rules out every direct cause and certifies a common cause; its maximum 3 is reached only by $|\Phi^+\rangle$.

check.question: What disproves identification of a target for a given design?
options: A wide confidence interval
A low training loss
Two allowed models with the same accessible data and different target values
A larger neural model that fits better
check.explanation: If two permitted models give identical data but different targets, no estimator can be consistent for both (Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-noest)). Loss, model size and interval width are properties of an estimate, not of identifiability.

check.question: With no assumptions beyond consistency, how wide is the interval for the ATE of a binary treatment on a binary outcome?
options: Exactly 1
Exactly 2
It shrinks to 0 with enough data
It depends on the sample size
check.explanation: The unseen terms range over $[0, P(x_0)]$ and $[0, P(x_1)]$, so the width is $P(x_0) + P(x_1) = 1$, whatever the sample size.

check.question: The same-basis correlation triple is $(1, 1, 1)$. Within the classes of Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-tetra), what produced it?
options: Neither; the triple is impossible
Either one; the data cannot tell
A direct cause, since every state has a sum of at most 1
A common cause, since only states reach the cube corners
check.explanation: Every state satisfies $c_{xx} + c_{yy} + c_{zz} \le 1$, and $(1, 1, 1)$ is the identity channel's vertex of the channel tetrahedron.

check.question: In a DAG with $Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$ and $X \to Y$, with $Z$ observed, which formula gives $P(y \mid \mathrm{do}(x))$?
options: $\sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\,P(z \mid x)$
$P(y \mid x)$
$\sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\,P(z)$
check.explanation: $Z$ blocks the only backdoor path, so adjustment averages the stratum-specific outcome over the marginal $P(z)$, not over $P(z \mid x)$.

misconceptions.claim: "A flexible enough model will eventually learn the causal effect from observational data."
misconceptions.correction: If two models in the class fit the data equally and disagree about the effect, Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-noest) shows no estimator can be consistent. Flexibility enlarges the class and can destroy identification.

misconceptions.claim: "Quantum data always identify causal structure."
misconceptions.correction: Only some triples do. Inside the octahedron $|c_1| + |c_2| + |c_3| \le 1$ both a state and a channel fit, and the classical common cause sits there. Restricting to one basis loses even that.

misconceptions.claim: "If the channel is identified, everything about the process is."
misconceptions.correction: Input-output data fix the channel but not its Kraus decomposition or environment; targets that depend on them need more structure or more access.

lessons.connect: Identification precedes the sample-complexity question of [L7-06](#lesson-l7-06): once a target is a function of the data, one can ask how many copies or shots estimate it to accuracy $\varepsilon$. The quantum part builds on informational access in [L6-05](#lesson-l6-05) and leads to the benchmark design of [L7-08](#lesson-l7-08), which must separate prediction from causal recovery.
lessons.caution: Every statement here is relative to a model class and a data map; enlarging either can break identification, and narrowing the class is an assumption the data cannot check. The classical examples assume binary variables, consistency and, for the backdoor repair, a known graph and positivity. The quantum theorem assumes a single common-cause state or a single direct cause with maximally mixed $A$, projective Pauli measurements with eigenstate re-preparation, and same-basis correlations only; mixtures of mechanisms, other preparations, or noisy and miscalibrated measurements change the sets. The code checks are numerical illustrations of the proofs, not experiments.

instructor.why: Research students often treat identification as an afterthought to model fitting. Putting a short impossibility theorem first, then classical and quantum counterexample pairs, makes the logical order explicit: target, class, data map, proof, then estimation [@pearlcausality; @bareinboim; @ried2015].
teaching_notes: Have students construct their own counterexample pair before showing M1 and M2; matching three numbers $P(X{=}1)$, $p_1$, $p_0$ is a short exercise.

The no-assumption bounds are due to Manski (1990); the sensitivity version used here is one simple parametrization among several. Use the sensitivity interactive to show that reporting an identified set as a function of an assumption is more informative than a point estimate with an unstated assumption.

Draw the two tetrahedra with physical models or the interactive figure; the duality (flip of the $YY$ axis) is easier to see than to read. Students met the theorem in [L6-05](#lesson-l6-05); spend the time on what is new here, the identification and partial-identification reading.
Ask which repairs change the data map and which change the model class; the distinction matters for what a referee can check.
instructor.assessment: The challenge on the tetrahedra tests whether students can use the inequalities as witnesses; the backdoor stretch exercise tests positivity; the worked example tests partial identification of a mixing weight.
instructor.extend: Read the experiment of [@ried2015] and identify which assumptions of Theorem [](#thm-l7-05-tetra) it relaxes. Then compare with the quantum causal model frameworks of [@allen] and [@barrett], and formulate an identification question for a three-node quantum causal model.

further.note: Experimental causal inference with quantum variables; shows that some quantum correlations reveal causal structure without intervention.
Process-based quantum causal modeling, including Markov conditions that define the model classes used for identification.
Identification and the causal hierarchy in a modern causal AI textbook.

lessons.title: Sample complexity and resource accounting
lessons.objective: Separate copies, queries, gates, depth, shots and classical cost; derive Hoeffding sample sizes with proof; and test whether a claimed quantum advantage survives once every resource is counted under a stated access model.
lessons.big_idea: A speedup is a statement about one resource under one access model; Hoeffding gives reproducible shot counts for fixed designs, and counting data loading, depth and noise can turn a quadratic or Heisenberg-type gain into nothing or into a constant factor.
outcomes: Prove Hoeffding's inequality from Hoeffding's lemma and compute $N \ge (2/\varepsilon^2)\ln(2/\delta)$ for one or many bounded means, stating the independence and fixed-design assumptions.
Classify the resources of a quantum procedure as copies, oracle queries, gates, depth, shots or classical processing, and say which comparison a claimed advantage concerns.
Show with Grover search that a query advantage survives for a computable oracle and vanishes for an unstructured classical table.
Derive the optimal number of coherent queries per shot under dephasing and explain why it gives a constant-factor gain instead of Heisenberg scaling.

key_terms.meaning: The number of copies of an unknown state or of independent observations needed to reach accuracy $\varepsilon$ with failure probability at most $\delta$.
The number of calls to an oracle (a black-box unitary or function), counting each call as one unit regardless of how it is implemented.
The number of elementary gates in a circuit, and the number of sequential layers; depth controls how long coherence must last.
The rules for how the algorithm reaches the data or the process: a computable function, a classical table, a quantum memory, copies of a state, or uses of a channel.
For a parametric family of outcome distributions, $F(\varphi) = \sum_x (\partial_\varphi p_x)^2/p_x$; by the Cramer-Rao inequality an unbiased estimator has variance at least $1/F$.

motivation: Grover's algorithm finds a marked item among $N = 2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$ with 804 oracle queries, against $N - 1 = 1{,}048{,}575$ in the worst case for a classical search. Is that a million-to-804 advantage? It depends on what an oracle query costs and where the items live. If they sit in an unsorted classical table, merely building the oracle reads all $N$ entries, and the advantage is gone.

Every quantum learning or causal-inference claim has the same structure: a count of one resource, under one access model, compared with a classical baseline. This lesson builds the tools to audit such claims: a precise list of resources, concentration bounds that turn accuracy into shot counts, and two worked audits in which an impressive scaling gain disappears or shrinks to a constant once data loading, depth and noise are counted [@nielsenchuang; @advantage].

sections.heading: Six resources that do not substitute for each other

blocks.title: Resources of a quantum procedure
blocks.label: def-l7-06-resources

blocks.mermaid:
graph LR

blocks.caption: A task fixes the accuracy and failure probability; the access model decides what one query costs and what must be loaded. Wall-clock cost depends on all of the resources.

blocks.title: Name the resource and the access model
blocks.md: "Exponential speedup" is not a sentence until it says: speedup in which resource, against which classical baseline, under which access model. Huang et al. show, for example, that classical learners given training data can match quantum models on some tasks where computing the quantum model alone is hard, so the comparison must count the data on both sides [@advantage].

sections.heading: Concentration: how many shots for one mean

blocks.title: Hoeffding's lemma
blocks.label: lem-l7-06-hl
blocks.md: If $a \le X \le b$ and $\mathbb{E}X = \mu$, then $\mathbb{E}\,e^{s(X - \mu)} \le e^{s^2(b-a)^2/8}$ for every real $s$ [@hoeffding1963].

By convexity of $e^{sx}$ on $[a, b]$, $e^{sX} \le \frac{b - X}{b - a}e^{sa} + \frac{X - a}{b - a}e^{sb}$. Take expectations and write $p = (\mu - a)/(b - a)$, $u = s(b - a)$: $\mathbb{E}\,e^{s(X-\mu)} \le e^{\phi(u)}$ with $\phi(u) = -pu + \ln(1 - p + pe^u)$. Then $\phi(0) = 0$, $\phi'(0) = 0$, and $\phi''(u) = q(1 - q)$ with $q = pe^u/(1 - p + pe^u) \in [0, 1]$, so $\phi'' \le 1/4$. Taylor's theorem gives $\phi(u) \le u^2/8 = s^2(b-a)^2/8$.

blocks.title: Hoeffding's inequality
blocks.label: thm-l7-06-hoeff
blocks.md:
Let $X_1, \dots, X_N$ be independent with $a \le X_i \le b$ and common mean $\mu$, and $\bar X_N = \frac1N\sum_i X_i$. For every $\varepsilon > 0$,

$$\Pr\big[\bar X_N - \mu \ge \varepsilon\big] \le e^{-2N\varepsilon^2/(b-a)^2}, \qquad \Pr\big[|\bar X_N - \mu| \ge \varepsilon\big] \le 2e^{-2N\varepsilon^2/(b-a)^2}.$$

For outcomes in $[-1, 1]$ the two-sided bound is $2e^{-N\varepsilon^2/2}$ [@hoeffding1963].

For $s > 0$, Markov's inequality applied to $e^{s(S_N - N\mu)}$ with $S_N = \sum_i X_i$ gives $\Pr[S_N - N\mu \ge N\varepsilon] \le e^{-sN\varepsilon}\,\mathbb{E}\,e^{s(S_N - N\mu)}$ (the Chernoff method [@coverthomas]). Independence factorizes the expectation into $\prod_i \mathbb{E}\,e^{s(X_i - \mu)}$, and Lemma [](#lem-l7-06-hl) bounds it by $e^{Ns^2(b-a)^2/8}$. The exponent $-sN\varepsilon + Ns^2(b-a)^2/8$ is smallest at $s = 4\varepsilon/(b-a)^2$, where it equals $-2N\varepsilon^2/(b-a)^2$. Apply the same argument to $-X_i$ and add the two tails.

blocks.alt: A probability bound transformed step by step from Markov's inequality to an exponential bound, then solved for the sample size 738.
blocks.caption: Markov, independence, Hoeffding's lemma, then the best $s$: the tail is at most $2e^{-N\varepsilon^2/2}$ for outcomes in $[-1, 1]$, and $\varepsilon = 0.1$, $\delta = 0.05$ need $N = 738$.
blocks.describe: The inequality $\Pr[S_N - N\mu \ge N\varepsilon] \le e^{-sN\varepsilon}\mathbb{E}e^{s(S_N - N\mu)}$ is written, labeled as Markov's inequality applied to an exponential. Its right side transforms term by term: independence turns the expectation into a product over $i$; Hoeffding's lemma bounds the product by $e^{Ns^2(b-a)^2/8}$; choosing $s = 4\varepsilon/(b-a)^2$ leaves $e^{-2N\varepsilon^2/(b-a)^2}$. For $[a, b] = [-1, 1]$ and two tails, the bound is $2e^{-N\varepsilon^2/2}$. Setting it at most $\delta$ gives $N \ge (2/\varepsilon^2)\ln(2/\delta)$, and for $\varepsilon = 0.1$, $\delta = 0.05$: $N \ge 200\ln 40 \approx 737.8$, so $N = 738$.

blocks.title: Sample size for one or many means
blocks.label: cor-l7-06-n
blocks.md: For outcomes in $[-1, 1]$, $N \ge \frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}\ln\frac{2}{\delta}$ shots give $|\bar X_N - \mu| < \varepsilon$ with probability at least $1 - \delta$. For $M$ means estimated from independent samples of size $N$ each, the union bound gives all $M$ within $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1 - \delta$ when $N \ge \frac{2}{\varepsilon^2}\ln\frac{2M}{\delta}$. With $\varepsilon = 0.1$, $\delta = 0.05$: $N = 738$ for one mean and $1659$ per mean for $M = 100$.

blocks.alt: Clouds of 200 sample means at increasing sample sizes, inside a violet Hoeffding band and a wider amber Chebyshev band; then running-mean paths, some of which cross the band.
blocks.caption: At each fixed $N$, almost all of 200 independent means lie inside the Hoeffding band. Running means are different: 11 percent of 400 paths leave the band somewhere, more than $\delta = 5$ percent.
blocks.describe: The horizontal axis is the sample size $N$ on a log scale from 10 to 10,000; the vertical axis is the error $\bar X_N - \mu$ for $\pm1$ outcomes with mean $0.2$. A violet band $\pm\sqrt{2\ln(2/\delta)/N}$ and a wider amber band $\pm\sqrt{1/(\delta N)}$ are drawn for $\delta = 0.05$. At $N = 30, 100, 300, 1000, 3000$ and $10{,}000$ a vertical cloud of 200 independent sample means appears, and a counter reports how many fall outside the Hoeffding band, at most a few each time. A dashed line marks $N = 738$, where the band half-width is $0.1$; the Chebyshev bound would need 2000. The clouds are then replaced by 24 running-mean paths, each adding one sample at a time; the red ones cross the band at some $N$. A note states that 11 percent of 400 such paths leave the band somewhere, more than $\delta$, because a guarantee for a fixed $N$ does not cover peeking at every $N$.

blocks.title: Chebyshev, the normal approximation, and what Hoeffding assumes
blocks.md: Chebyshev's inequality needs only a variance bound and gives $N \ge 1/(\delta\varepsilon^2) = 2000$, worse in its $1/\delta$ dependence than Hoeffding's $\ln(2/\delta)$. The normal approximation with variance at most 1, $N \approx z_{1-\delta/2}^2/\varepsilon^2 = 385$, is smaller but is not a bound for finite $N$. Hoeffding's guarantee assumes independent, bounded outcomes and a sample size fixed in advance. Drift in the device breaks independence, and choosing $N$ after looking at the data (optional stopping) breaks the fixed design, as the animation shows; sequential designs need time-uniform bounds instead.

blocks.caption: Choose the failure probability $\delta$. Curves give the samples needed for accuracy $\varepsilon$ by Hoeffding, by Chebyshev, by the normal approximation (not a bound), and by Hoeffding for 100 means at once.
blocks.describe: A log-log plot of the required number of samples $N$ against the accuracy $\varepsilon$ from 0.005 to 0.5 for outcomes in $[-1, 1]$. All curves fall as $1/\varepsilon^2$. At $\delta = 0.05$ and $\varepsilon = 0.1$ the values are 738 (Hoeffding), 2000 (Chebyshev), 385 (normal approximation) and 1659 per mean for 100 simultaneous means. Moving the slider to $\delta = 10^{-6}$ raises the Hoeffding curve only by the factor $\ln(2\times10^6)/\ln 40 \approx 3.9$, while the Chebyshev curve rises by a factor of 50,000 and passes far above the others.

blocks.title: Shadow estimates of a Pauli string
blocks.label: prop-l7-06-shadow
blocks.md: Measure every qubit in a uniformly random Pauli basis. For a Pauli string $P$ of weight $k$, the single-snapshot estimate $\hat X = \prod_{j \in \mathrm{supp}P} 3\,b_j\,\mathbf{1}[\text{basis}_j = P_j]$ (with outcomes $b_j = \pm1$) satisfies $\mathbb{E}\hat X = \operatorname{Tr}(\rho P)$ and $\mathbb{E}\hat X^2 = 3^k$.

Sketch: the bases match $P$ on its support with probability $3^{-k}$, and then $\hat X = 3^k\prod_j b_j$ with conditional mean $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho P)$; otherwise $\hat X = 0$. So $\mathbb{E}\hat X = \operatorname{Tr}(\rho P)$ and $\mathbb{E}\hat X^2 = 3^{-k}\cdot 9^k = 3^k$. The inverse channel behind this estimator, the full proof and the Huang-Kueng-Preskill guarantee are developed in [L7-07](#lesson-l7-07) [@shadows].

blocks.title: What the range-based bound says about shadows
blocks.md: Since $\hat X \in [-3^k, 3^k]$, Hoeffding needs $N \ge 2\cdot9^k\ln(2M/\delta)/\varepsilon^2$ snapshots for $M$ such strings at once; measuring each string directly costs $M\cdot 2\ln(2M/\delta)/\varepsilon^2$ shots in total. With these bounds shadows win when $M > 9^k$. Median-of-means estimators, as used by Huang, Kueng and Preskill, replace the range factor $9^k$ by the variance $3^k$ at the price of larger constants ([L7-07](#lesson-l7-07)). Either way the saving depends on the observables, not only on their number.

sections.heading: Queries, gates and data access: auditing Grover

blocks.title: Grover success probability
blocks.label: prop-l7-06-grover
blocks.md: With one marked item among $N$ and $\sin\theta = 1/\sqrt N$, after $k$ Grover iterations (each one oracle query) the probability of measuring the marked item is $\sin^2\big((2k + 1)\theta\big)$. Taking $k = \lfloor \pi/(4\theta) \rfloor$ gives success probability at least $1 - 1/N$; for $N = 2^{20}$ this is $k = 804$ [@grover1996].

The state stays in the plane spanned by the marked state $|w\rangle$ and the uniform superposition of the others, $|r\rangle$. The start is $\sin\theta|w\rangle + \cos\theta|r\rangle$. The oracle reflects about $|r\rangle$ and the diffusion step reflects about the start; two reflections make a rotation by $2\theta$, so after $k$ iterations the angle from $|r\rangle$ is $(2k+1)\theta$ [@nielsenchuang]. With $k = \lfloor\pi/(4\theta)\rfloor$ the final angle is within $\theta$ of $\pi/2$, so the failure probability is at most $\sin^2\theta = 1/N$. For $N = 2^{20}$, $\pi/(4\theta) \approx 804.2$.

Grover's query count is optimal up to a constant factor: any quantum algorithm needs order $\sqrt N$ queries to an unstructured oracle [@bbbv1997; @nielsenchuang]. A deterministic classical search needs $N - 1 = 1{,}048{,}575$ queries in the worst case, and a randomized one about $N/2$ on average. The gap in queries is real. Whether it is a gap in cost depends on the access model.

blocks.alt: Two bars on a log scale, classical at about one million queries and quantum at 804; under a classical-table access model the quantum bar grows past the classical one.
blocks.caption: Grover on $2^{20}$ items: 804 queries against 1,048,575. If the oracle is a circuit for a computable predicate the gap survives; if the items are in a classical table, loading them costs $N$ and the advantage vanishes.
blocks.describe: The task is to find one marked item among $N = 2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$. A log-scale bar chart shows the classical worst-case count $N - 1 = 1{,}048{,}575$ and the Grover count $\lfloor\pi/(4\theta)\rfloor = 804$ with $\sin\theta = 2^{-10}$. Access model A is stated: the predicate $f$ is a circuit we can run, so both costs scale as queries times the cost $c_f$ of one evaluation plus a few gates, and the quadratic gap survives. Access model B follows: the items sit in a classical table, and building the oracle reads all $N$ entries. The quantum bar grows to $804 + 1{,}048{,}576 = 1{,}049{,}380$, above the classical bar. The closing line: same task and algorithm, but the access model decides the advantage.

blocks.caption: For $N = 2^{10}$ the success probability peaks at $k = 25$ queries and then falls: queries are not a monotone resource. The classical curve $k/N$ is the chance that $k$ random distinct queries include the marked item.

blocks.title: Loading cost and quantum memory
blocks.md: Any procedure that builds an oracle from an unstructured classical table of $N$ entries must read every entry at least once, because an entry it never reads cannot affect the oracle. A quantum random-access memory could amortize that cost over many searches of the same table, but it is hardware with order $N$ components, and its preparation, error rates and depth then enter the ledger.

sections.heading: Queries versus depth: phase estimation under dephasing

blocks.md: To learn a phase $\varphi$ from a unitary $e^{-i\varphi Z/2}$, each shot applies it $k$ times in sequence to $|+\rangle$ and measures $X$; outcome $0$ is the $+1$ eigenvalue of $X$. With dephasing that shrinks coherence by $e^{-\gamma}$ per query, the outcome probability is

blocks.latex: P(0 \mid \varphi) = \tfrac12\big(1 + V\cos k\varphi\big), \qquad V = e^{-\gamma k}.
blocks.label: eq-l7-06-pk

blocks.title: Fisher information per shot
blocks.label: prop-l7-06-fisher
blocks.md: For [](#eq-l7-06-pk), $F_{\text{shot}}(\varphi) = \dfrac{k^2V^2\sin^2 k\varphi}{1 - V^2\cos^2 k\varphi} \le k^2V^2 = k^2e^{-2\gamma k}$, with equality where $\cos k\varphi = 0$.

For two outcomes, $F = (\partial_\varphi P)^2/(P(1-P))$. Here $\partial_\varphi P = -\tfrac12 kV\sin k\varphi$ and $P(1 - P) = \tfrac14(1 - V^2\cos^2 k\varphi)$. Since $V \le 1$, $1 - V^2\cos^2 \ge 1 - \cos^2 = \sin^2$, so the ratio is at most $k^2V^2$, with equality when $\cos k\varphi = 0$.

blocks.title: The best depth under a fixed query budget
blocks.label: cor-l7-06-opt
blocks.md: With $Q$ queries in total and $Q/k$ independent shots, Fisher information adds: $F_{\text{tot}} \le Qk\,e^{-2\gamma k}$. This is largest at $k^\star = \frac{1}{2\gamma}$, where $F_{\max} = \frac{Q}{2e\gamma}$. By the Cramer-Rao inequality, any unbiased estimator then has $\delta\varphi \ge \sqrt{2e\gamma/Q}$ [@coverthomas]. Without dephasing, $F_{\text{tot}} = Qk$ grows with $k$; a single shot with $k = Q$ reaches $Q^2$, the Heisenberg scaling $\delta\varphi \sim 1/Q$.

blocks.alt: Curves of Fisher information per query against queries per shot, rising then falling, with a red dot at the peak that moves right as the dephasing rate decreases.
blocks.caption: Fisher information per query $k e^{-2\gamma k}$: it follows the noiseless line $k$ only until $k^\star = \frac{1}{2\gamma}$. The best total is $\frac{Q}{2e\gamma}$: a constant-factor gain over repetition, not Heisenberg scaling.
blocks.describe: The model $P(0 \mid \varphi) = \frac12(1 + e^{-\gamma k}\cos k\varphi)$ and the bound $F_{\text{shot}} \le k^2e^{-2\gamma k}$ are written. A log-log plot shows Fisher information per query against queries per shot $k$ from 1 to about 5000. A gray line is the noiseless value $k$. A violet curve $ke^{-2\gamma k}$ follows it for small $k$, peaks, and falls; a red dot marks the peak at $k^\star = 1/(2\gamma)$ with height $1/(2e\gamma)$. As $\gamma$ decreases from 0.1 to 0.001, the peak moves from $k = 5$ (height about 1.8) to $k = 500$ (height about 184); it settles at $\gamma = 0.01$ with $k^\star = 50$ and $F/Q \approx 18.4$. The derivation $F_{\text{tot}} = (Q/k)k^2e^{-2\gamma k} = Qke^{-2\gamma k}$, $k^\star = 1/(2\gamma)$, $F_{\max} = Q/(2e\gamma)$ and $\delta\varphi \ge \sqrt{2e\gamma/Q}$ follows, with the remark that the error still scales as $1/\sqrt Q$.

blocks.caption: Change the dephasing per query $\gamma$. The red marker is the optimal number of sequential queries per shot and the information per query it achieves.
blocks.describe: A log-log plot of Fisher information per query against queries per shot $k$ from 1 to 5000. The dashed gray line $F/Q = k$ is the noiseless case. The violet curve is $ke^{-2\gamma k}$ for the chosen $\gamma$ and the red marker its maximum at $k = 1/(2\gamma)$, height $1/(2e\gamma)$. At $\gamma = 0.1$ the marker is at $k = 5$, height $1.84$; at $\gamma = 0.01$, $k = 50$, height $18.4$; at $\gamma = 0.0005$, $k = 1000$, height $368$. At $\gamma = 0$ the curve coincides with the dashed line and the marker moves to the right edge: with no dephasing deeper shots always help.

blocks.title: What this toy does and does not show
blocks.md: The Fisher information is a local quantity: with $k > 1$, $k\varphi$ is known only modulo $2\pi$, so reaching the bound needs prior knowledge of $\varphi$ to within $\pi/k$ or an adaptive multi-round scheme, and the Cramer-Rao bound is approached only with many shots. The dephasing model is a single assumed rate per query. Within these assumptions the lesson is robust: a query advantage that needs coherent depth is limited by the coherence time. A general theorem of this kind exists for parallel strategies: Demkowicz-Dobrzanski, Kolodynski and Guta prove that for generic uncorrelated noise, including dephasing, entangled probes improve the asymptotic precision over independent probes only by a constant factor, not in scaling [@demkowicz2012]. The sequential toy model here shows the same effect; it is not an instance of their theorem.

sections.heading: Reading an advantage claim

blocks.title: Resource audit of a claim
blocks.label: alg-l7-06-audit
blocks.md:
1. State the task, the accuracy $\varepsilon$ and the failure probability $\delta$.
2. State the access model on both sides: how data or the process are reached, and what one query costs.
3. Count copies, queries, gates, depth, shots and classical processing separately, with their scaling.
4. Derive shot counts from a stated concentration bound and its assumptions (independence, fixed design, number of simultaneous estimates).
5. Include loading, compilation and noise: for each, say whether it changes the scaling or a constant.
6. Compare with the best known classical method under the same access, including one that uses the same data.

blocks.explain: Hoeffding sample sizes, a Monte Carlo check of the guarantee, and the optional-stopping effect from the animation. The paths here use a different random seed from the animation, so the fraction that leaves the band differs from its 11 percent; either way it is well above $\delta = 0.05$.
blocks.source:
import math
import numpy as np

def n_hoeffding(eps, delta, width=2.0, m=1):
    """N >= width^2 ln(2m/delta) / (2 eps^2): m means, each within eps, all at once w.p. >= 1 - delta."""
    return math.ceil(width ** 2 * math.log(2 * m / delta) / (2 * eps ** 2))

eps, delta = 0.1, 0.05
print("Hoeffding:", n_hoeffding(eps, delta), "  exact value 200 ln 40 =", round(200 * math.log(40), 2))
print("Chebyshev (variance <= 1):", math.ceil(1 / (delta * eps ** 2)))
print("Hoeffding, 100 means at once:", n_hoeffding(eps, delta, m=100), "per mean")

# Monte Carlo: how often is a mean of N = 738 outcomes (+-1, mean 0.2) off by 0.1 or more?
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
N, trials, mu = 738, 20000, 0.2
k = rng.binomial(N, (1 + mu) / 2, size=trials)          # number of +1 outcomes
means = (2 * k - N) / N
print("observed failure rate:", (np.abs(means - mu) >= eps).mean(), " (guaranteed <= 0.05; the bound is conservative)")

# running means: how many paths leave the fixed-N band somewhere between N = 10 and N = 10000?
x = np.where(rng.random((400, 10000)) < (1 + mu) / 2, 1.0, -1.0)
run = np.cumsum(x, axis=1) / np.arange(1, 10001)
band = np.sqrt(2 * math.log(2 / delta) / np.arange(1, 10001))
ever = (np.abs(run - mu) >= band)[:, 9:].any(axis=1).mean()
print(f"fraction of 400 running-mean paths that ever leave the band: {ever:.3f}  (not <= 0.05)")

blocks.explain: The shadow, Grover and dephased phase-estimation ledgers, computed from their formulas and checked numerically.
blocks.source:
# Classical shadows for one weight-k Pauli string: the single-snapshot estimator takes values 0 or +-3^k
for k in (1, 2, 3, 4):
    print(f"weight {k}: E[X^2] = 3^{k} = {3 ** k:3d};  range-based Hoeffding factor 9^{k} = {9 ** k}")

# Grover on N items: iterations, success probability, and the ledger with a classical table
for n in (10, 20, 30):
    Nn = 2 ** n
    th = math.asin(1 / math.sqrt(Nn))
    kq = math.floor(math.pi / (4 * th))
    print(f"N = 2^{n}: Grover {kq:,} queries (success {math.sin((2 * kq + 1) * th) ** 2:.6f});"
          f" classical worst case {Nn - 1:,}; with table loading {kq + Nn:,}")

# Phase estimation with dephasing: Fisher information per query k exp(-2 gamma k), maximized over k
for gamma in (0.1, 0.01, 0.001):
    ks = np.arange(1, 20001)
    f = ks * np.exp(-2 * gamma * ks)
    print(f"gamma = {gamma}: best k = {ks[f.argmax()]} (1/(2 gamma) = {1 / (2 * gamma):g}),"
          f" F/Q = {f.max():.2f} (1/(2 e gamma) = {1 / (2 * math.e * gamma):.2f})")

# the per-shot bound F <= k^2 V^2, attained at cos(k phi) = 0
k, V = 7, math.exp(-0.01 * 7)
ph = np.linspace(0.01, math.pi / k - 0.01, 2000)
F = (k * V * np.sin(k * ph)) ** 2 / (1 - (V * np.cos(k * ph)) ** 2)
print("max over phi of F:", round(F.max(), 4), " k^2 V^2 =", round(k * k * V * V, 4))

worked_example.title: Budget for a causal-effect estimate on hardware
worked_example.problem: A study estimates 50 expectation values of $\pm1$ observables, each to accuracy $\varepsilon = 0.02$, all simultaneously with failure probability $\delta = 0.01$, by measuring each one directly with independent shots. Each shot takes 200 microseconds including reset. How many shots per observable, how many in total, and how long does data collection take? Which costs does this omit?
steps: Union bound with $M = 50$: $N \ge \frac{2}{0.02^2}\ln\frac{2\cdot50}{0.01} = 5000\ln(10^4) \approx 5000 \times 9.2103 = 46{,}051.7$, so $N = 46{,}052$ shots per observable.
Time: $2{,}302{,}600 \times 200\,\mu\text{s} \approx 460.5$ s, under 8 minutes of pure shot time.

Omitted: calibration and drift checks (drift breaks the independence that Hoeffding needs), compilation, classical post-processing, and above all the identification step of [L7-05](#lesson-l7-05): accurate means of the wrong quantities do not give a causal effect.
worked_example.result: $46{,}052$ shots per observable and about $2.3$ million in total, roughly 8 minutes of shot time, valid only for independent shots with a sample size fixed in advance.

exercises.prompt: Use $\varepsilon = 0.2$ and $\delta = 0.1$ for one $\pm1$ mean. Find the Hoeffding sample size and say what it does not measure.
exercises.solution: $N \ge \frac{2}{0.04}\ln 20 = 50\ln 20 \approx 149.79$, so $N = 150$. It counts independent shots for one observable; it does not count gates, depth, state preparation time, compilation, or the extra samples needed for several observables or adaptive stopping.

exercises.prompt: Compute the Grover iteration count $\lfloor\pi/(4\theta)\rfloor$ and success probability for $N = 2^{10}$, and the classical worst-case query count.
exercises.solution: $\theta = \arcsin(2^{-5}) \approx 0.031255$, so $\pi/(4\theta) \approx 25.13$ and $k = 25$. Success $\sin^2(51\theta) \approx \sin^2(1.59400) \approx 0.99946$. Classical worst case $N - 1 = 1023$.

exercises.prompt: Show that Hoeffding's bound for outcomes in $\{0, 1\}$ with mean $p$ gives $N \ge \ln(2/\delta)/(2\varepsilon^2)$, and compare with the $[-1, 1]$ formula. Why are they consistent?
exercises.solution: With $b - a = 1$, $2e^{-2N\varepsilon^2} \le \delta$ gives $N \ge \ln(2/\delta)/(2\varepsilon^2)$. Mapping $Y = 2X - 1 \in [-1, 1]$ doubles both the range and the error: accuracy $\varepsilon$ for $X$ is accuracy $2\varepsilon$ for $Y$, and $(2/(2\varepsilon)^2)\ln(2/\delta) = \ln(2/\delta)/(2\varepsilon^2)$.

exercises.prompt: In the dephased phase-estimation model, compare $k = 1$ with $k^\star$ for $\gamma = 0.001$: by what factor does the optimal depth reduce the number of queries needed for a target $\delta\varphi$?
exercises.solution: Required queries scale as $1/(\delta\varphi^2 \cdot F/Q)$. At $k = 1$, $F/Q = e^{-0.002} \approx 0.998$. At $k^\star = 500$, $F/Q = 1/(2e\cdot0.001) \approx 183.9$. The optimal depth needs about $184$ times fewer queries: a large constant factor, but the scaling in $\delta\varphi$ is still $1/\delta\varphi^2$.

exercises.prompt: A paper reports estimating all $M = 10^4$ two-qubit Pauli strings of a 20-qubit state from classical shadows, versus measuring each directly. Using the range-based Hoeffding bounds of Proposition [](#prop-l7-06-shadow), with $\varepsilon = 0.05$ and $\delta = 0.01$, compute both shot totals and decide which wins. Then redo the comparison for weight-6 strings.
exercises.solution: Common factor $c = 2\ln(2M/\delta)/\varepsilon^2 = 800\ln(2\times10^6) \approx 800\times14.509 = 11{,}607$. Direct: $M c \approx 1.16\times10^8$ shots. Shadows, weight 2: $9^2 c = 81c \approx 9.40\times10^5$ snapshots for all strings at once, so shadows win by a factor of about 123 $(= 10^4/81)$. Weight 6: $9^6 = 531{,}441 > M$, so shadows need about $6.17\times10^9$ snapshots and direct measurement wins under these bounds. Variance-based estimators replace $9^6$ by $3^6 = 729 < 10^4$, but with the constants of the Huang-Kueng-Preskill theorem ([L7-07](#lesson-l7-07)) the budget is $KN$ with $K = \lceil 2\ln(2\times10^6)\rceil = 30$ and $N = \lceil 34\cdot729/0.05^2\rceil = 9{,}914{,}400$, about $2.97\times10^8$ snapshots, so direct measurement still wins, by a factor of about 2.6, under those conservative constants. Only if the constants were near 1 would $729 < 10^4$ favor shadows. The conclusion depends on the estimator, its constants and the observable weight.

exercises.prompt: Prove that a procedure which builds a membership oracle for an arbitrary subset of an $N$-element classical table must read all $N$ entries in the worst case.
exercises.solution: Suppose for some input table the procedure never reads entry $j$. Change only entry $j$ (flip its membership). The procedure's reads, and hence its output oracle, are identical for both tables, because its behavior depends only on what it reads. But the correct oracles differ on $j$. So on one of the two tables the output is wrong. Hence a correct procedure reads every entry of every table, at least $N$ reads.

check.question: Which statement about resource counts is correct?
options: A small shot count guarantees a low total cost
Each count needs its own stated access and cost model
Queries, copies and wall-clock time are interchangeable
Gate count does not depend on the access model
check.explanation: Different resource measures describe different operations. An algorithm can save queries while spending more on loading, depth or classical processing, so a comparison must state its model.

check.question: How does the Hoeffding sample size depend on the failure probability $\delta$ at fixed accuracy?
options: As $1/\delta$
It does not depend on $\delta$
As $1/\delta^2$
Logarithmically, through $\ln(2/\delta)$
check.explanation: $N \ge (2/\varepsilon^2)\ln(2/\delta)$. Chebyshev's bound, using only the variance, grows as $1/\delta$.

check.question: Why does Grover's query advantage vanish for data stored in an unstructured classical table?
options: The success probability is too low
Grover needs more than $N$ queries
Classical search becomes faster than $N$
Building the oracle requires reading all $N$ entries
check.explanation: An entry that is never read cannot affect the oracle, so the loading step alone costs $N$ reads, more than the classical worst case of $N - 1$ queries.

check.question: A 95 percent confidence interval procedure is applied to many independent experiments. What does 95 percent describe?
options: The probability that the true value is in this particular interval after it is computed
The probability that the next measurement falls in the interval
The fraction of intervals, over repetitions, that contain the true value
The fraction of data inside the interval
check.explanation: The coverage is a property of the procedure over repetitions. Hoeffding intervals have the same frequentist meaning, and only for a sample size fixed in advance.

misconceptions.claim: "A quadratic or exponential query speedup is a speedup in running time."
misconceptions.correction: Only if a query costs about the same in both models and nothing else dominates. Data loading, oracle construction, depth and error correction can change or erase the gap.

misconceptions.claim: "If the error bar is small after N shots, I can stop there."
misconceptions.correction: Stopping when the estimate looks good is optional stopping: a fixed-$N$ bound no longer applies, and the failure probability can be several times $\delta$, as the 11 percent in the band animation shows.

misconceptions.claim: "Classical shadows estimate any number of observables with logarithmic cost."
misconceptions.correction: The logarithm is in $M$, but each observable's cost carries a factor such as $3^k$ (variance) or $9^k$ (range) that grows exponentially with its weight. High-weight observables can cost more than direct measurement.

misconceptions.claim: "Heisenberg scaling means quantum sensors are quadratically better in practice."
misconceptions.correction: With dephasing per query, the optimal depth is $1/(2\gamma)$ and the gain becomes a constant factor $1/(2e\gamma)$ over repetition; the error scales as $1/\sqrt{Q}$ again.

lessons.connect: Shot budgets for gradients in [L7-04](#lesson-l7-04) are an instance of Corollary [](#cor-l7-06-n). Classical shadows, where the cost depends on the observables, are developed in [L7-07](#lesson-l7-07), and the reproducible benchmark design of [L7-08](#lesson-l7-08) requires the resource audit of this lesson.
lessons.caution: Hoeffding's inequality assumes independent, bounded outcomes and a sample size fixed before seeing data; drift, adaptive stopping and post-selection need other bounds. The Grover ledger counts reads and queries, not gate-level costs, and the classical-table argument concerns building the oracle once. The phase-estimation model assumes a single dephasing rate per query and uses a local Fisher-information bound that needs prior knowledge or adaptivity to reach. Nothing here proves or disproves a quantum advantage for a specific application; it shows how to state and check one.

instructor.why: Advantage claims at the research frontier are often stated in one resource while the costs lie in another. Proving Hoeffding, auditing Grover under two access models, and showing how dephasing caps the benefit of depth give students a reusable checklist for reading and writing such claims [@nielsenchuang; @coverthomas; @advantage].
teaching_notes: Ask students to guess, before the band animation, what fraction of running-mean paths leaves a 95 percent band; most guess 5 percent.
Have pairs audit a recent quantum machine learning abstract with the six-step algorithm; insist that every count has a stated access model.
Use the Grover figure to show that queries are not monotone: running the search longer can lower the success probability.
In the phase-estimation part, emphasize that the conclusion is about scaling; large constant-factor gains can still matter in practice.
instructor.assessment: The first challenge exercise tests whether students can carry a resource comparison through with explicit bounds and notice the dependence on observable weight; the second tests the lower-bound argument for data loading.
instructor.extend: Replace Hoeffding by a Bernstein-type bound that uses the variance, and recompute the shadow comparison with $3^k$ instead of $9^k$. Read the data-dependent comparisons in [@advantage] and identify which resource each comparison holds fixed.

further.note: Classical shadows, with sample complexity that depends on the measurement ensemble and on the observables.
How classical access to training data changes quantum learning comparisons.
A quantum causal inference protocol designed for a specific two-time measurement setting; a good test case for this lesson's resource audit.

lessons.title: Classical shadows and observable structure
lessons.objective: Derive the classical-shadow estimator for random Pauli measurements, compute its exact cost for Pauli observables, and use the Huang-Kueng-Preskill theorem to decide which families of observables a shadow can estimate cheaply.
lessons.big_idea: A classical shadow inverts the average effect of a random measurement, so one data set estimates many observables; the price of each observable is its shadow norm, which for random Pauli measurements grows like 3 to the power of its weight, not with the number of observables or qubits.
outcomes: Derive the single-qubit measurement channel $\mathcal{M}(\rho) = \rho/3 + \operatorname{Tr}(\rho)\, I/3$, its inverse, and the snapshot $3U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U - I$, and explain why a snapshot is unbiased but not a state.
Prove that the random-Pauli estimator of a weight-$k$ Pauli string has single-snapshot variance exactly $3^k - \langle P\rangle^2$, and turn it into a snapshot budget for a stated error.
State the Huang-Kueng-Preskill median-of-means theorem with its constants, compute $K$, $N$ and $NK$ for a family of observables, and say what the constants do and do not mean.
Decide, for a given observable family, whether random Pauli or random Clifford shadows (or a direct measurement) are the efficient choice, using shadow-norm bounds and the matching lower bounds.

key_terms.meaning: A list of $N$ snapshots $\hat\rho_i = \mathcal{M}^{-1}(U_i^\dagger|b_i\rangle\langle b_i|U_i)$ built from random measurements; it predicts linear functions $\operatorname{Tr}(O\rho)$ chosen after the data are taken.
One inverted measurement record. It has unit trace and expectation $\rho$, but it can have negative eigenvalues.
The map $\mathcal{M}$ obtained by averaging $U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U$ over the random unitary and the Born-rule outcome; it must be invertible (tomographic completeness).
The ensemble-dependent norm $\|O\|_{\mathrm{shadow}}$ that bounds the single-snapshot variance of $\operatorname{Tr}(O\hat\rho)$ for every state.
The number of qubits on which an observable acts non-trivially; a Pauli string such as $Z\otimes Z\otimes I$ has weight 2.
Split the data into $K$ groups, average within each group, report the median of the group means; it turns a variance bound into an exponentially small failure probability.

motivation: Suppose a 20-qubit device prepares a state and you want every one- and two-body Pauli expectation value: there are $3\cdot 20 + 9\cdot\binom{20}{2} = 1770$ of them. Full tomography of 20 qubits is hopeless, because a density operator has $4^{20} - 1 \approx 10^{12}$ real parameters ([L5-09](#lesson-l5-09)). Measuring each Pauli in its own basis works but spends a separate budget on every observable. Huang, Kueng and Preskill showed a third way: measure in random bases, store the outcomes, and estimate all 1770 numbers from one data set, with a measurement count that grows only with the logarithm of the number of observables [@shadows].

That sentence is often quoted as if classical shadows estimated anything cheaply. They do not. The same theorem says the cost of each observable is set by its shadow norm, which depends on the measurement ensemble and on the structure of the observable. For random Pauli measurements a weight-$k$ Pauli string costs $3^k$ per snapshot, so a 50-qubit parity costs $3^{50} \approx 7.2\times 10^{23}$ while measuring it directly costs order $1/\epsilon^2$. This lesson derives the estimator, proves the exact cost of Pauli observables, states the theorem with its constants, and trains the habit this level needs: before believing a resource claim, find the norm that controls it ([L7-06](#lesson-l7-06)).

sections.heading: A measurement you undo on paper

blocks.md: Prepare the unknown $n$-qubit state $\rho$, apply a unitary $U$ drawn at random from a fixed ensemble $\mathcal{U}$, and measure every qubit in the computational basis, obtaining the bit string $b$. Store a classical description of $U$ and $b$. Repeat with fresh copies. Each record is cheap; the question is how to turn the records into estimates of $\operatorname{Tr}(O\rho)$ for observables $O$ that you may choose only later.

blocks.title: Measurement primitive, measurement channel and classical shadow
blocks.label: def-l7-07-shadow
blocks.md: A **measurement primitive** is an ensemble $\mathcal{U}$ of unitaries followed by a computational-basis measurement, with outcome probabilities $\Pr[b] = \langle b|U\rho U^\dagger|b\rangle$. It is **tomographically complete** if for every $\sigma \ne \rho$ some $U \in \mathcal{U}$ and $b$ give $\langle b|U\sigma U^\dagger|b\rangle \ne \langle b|U\rho U^\dagger|b\rangle$. The **measurement channel** is the average in [](#eq-l7-07-channel). A **snapshot** is $\hat\rho = \mathcal{M}^{-1}(U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U)$, and a **classical shadow of size $N$** is the list $\hat\rho_1, \dots, \hat\rho_N$ from $N$ independent repetitions [@shadows].

The last identity is linearity: $\mathbb{E}[U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U] = \mathcal{M}(\rho)$ by definition, and $\mathcal{M}^{-1}$ is a fixed linear map, so it commutes with the expectation. Tomographic completeness is exactly what makes $\mathcal{M}$ invertible as a linear map. The inverse is not a physical operation (it is not completely positive); it is classical post-processing applied to stored data [@shadows]. Throughout this lesson qubit 1 is the leftmost tensor factor, and a bit $b_j$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $1 - 2b_j = \pm 1$.

blocks.title: Single-qubit random Pauli shadows
blocks.label: prop-l7-07-onequbit
blocks.md: Let $U$ be $H$, $HS^\dagger$ or $I$ with probability $1/3$ each, so that the measurement is in the $X$, $Y$ or $Z$ eigenbasis. Then for every operator $X$ on one qubit (here $X$ denotes an arbitrary operator, not the Pauli matrix), $\mathcal{M}(X) = \tfrac13 X + \tfrac13\operatorname{Tr}(X)\, I$ and $\mathcal{M}^{-1}(X) = 3X - \operatorname{Tr}(X)\, I$. The snapshot is $\hat\rho = 3U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U - I$. If the basis is $P \in \{X, Y, Z\}$ and the outcome eigenvalue is $b = \pm 1$, then $\hat\rho = \tfrac12(I + 3b\,P)$: its Bloch vector is $3\,b\,\vec e_P$, of length 3, and its eigenvalues are $2$ and $-1$.

Write $\rho = \tfrac12(I + \vec r\cdot\vec\sigma)$. In basis $P$ the two projectors are $\tfrac12(I \pm P)$ with probabilities $\tfrac12(1 \pm r_P)$, so $\sum_{\pm} \tfrac12(1 \pm r_P)\,\tfrac12(I \pm P) = \tfrac12(I + r_P P)$. Averaging over the three bases gives $\mathcal{M}(\rho) = \tfrac13\sum_P \tfrac12(I + r_P P) = \tfrac{I}{2} + \tfrac{\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma}{6} = \tfrac13\rho + \tfrac13 I$. Both sides are linear in $\rho$, and the trace-one operators span all operators, so $\mathcal{M}(A) = \tfrac13 A + \tfrac13\operatorname{Tr}(A) I$ for every operator $A$. Solving $C = \tfrac13 A + \tfrac13\operatorname{Tr}(A) I$ for $A$: the trace gives $\operatorname{Tr} C = \operatorname{Tr} A$, hence $A = 3C - \operatorname{Tr}(C) I$. Apply this to the rank-one projector $U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U = \tfrac12(I + bP)$, which has trace 1: $\hat\rho = \tfrac32(I + bP) - I = \tfrac12(I + 3bP)$. Its eigenvalues are $\tfrac12(1 \pm 3)$, that is $2$ and $-1$. Finally $\mathbb{E}[3b\,\vec e_P] = \sum_P \tfrac13 \cdot 3\,r_P\,\vec e_P = \vec r$.

blocks.alt: A Bloch ball with a violet state vector, six amber points at distance 3 on the coordinate axes, and a cyan running average that wanders from those points toward the violet vector as random snapshots arrive.
blocks.caption: Every single-qubit snapshot lands on one of six points at Bloch radius 3, outside the ball. Only their running average approaches the state.
blocks.describe: A Bloch ball of radius 1 is drawn with the state's Bloch vector $\vec r = (0.4, 0.3, 0.6)$ in violet. Six amber points sit on the axes at distance 3: these are the only possible snapshots. The formulas $\hat\rho = 3U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U - I$ and the Bloch vector $3\,b\,\vec e_P$ appear, with the example $Z$, $b = +1$: $\hat\rho = \operatorname{diag}(2,-1)$, eigenvalues 2 and $-1$, so a snapshot is not a state. Then 240 seeded snapshots arrive one at a time; each flashes in red at one of the six points, and a cyan dot tracks the running average. A counter shows $N$ and the distance from the average to $\vec r$, which shrinks as $N$ grows. The scene ends with $\mathbb{E}[\hat\rho] = \rho$: only the average is a state.

blocks.alt: A cross-section of the Bloch ball shrinks to one third of its size while a derivation of the measurement channel is written; then a boundary point is stretched by a factor of 3 to a point outside the disk.
blocks.caption: The randomized measurement, averaged, is a depolarizing contraction by $1/3$; the snapshot undoes it on paper, which pushes single records to radius 3.
blocks.describe: On the left is the $x$-$z$ cross-section of the Bloch ball with the state $\rho$. On the right the derivation is written and transformed term by term: $\mathcal{M}(\rho) = \mathbb{E}_U \sum_b \langle b|U\rho U^\dagger|b\rangle\,U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U$, then $\tfrac13\sum_P \tfrac12(I + r_P P)$, then $\tfrac{I}{2} + \tfrac{\vec r\cdot\vec\sigma}{6}$, then $\tfrac13\rho + \tfrac13\operatorname{Tr}(\rho) I$. The disk shrinks to radius $1/3$ and the state moves to $\vec r/3$. The inverse $\mathcal{M}^{-1}(X) = 3X - \operatorname{Tr}(X)\, I$ appears in red, followed by the snapshot $3U^\dagger|b\rangle\langle b|U - I$. The projector $|0\rangle\langle 0|$ on the disk's edge is stretched by 3 to the point $\operatorname{diag}(2,-1)$ outside the disk, and the other snapshot points at radius 3 appear.

blocks.title: Do not repair each snapshot
blocks.md: It is tempting to replace each snapshot by the nearest physical state. For one qubit the nearest pure state to $\tfrac12(I + 3bP)$ is $\tfrac12(I + bP)$, and its average is $\sum_P \tfrac13 r_P \vec e_P = \vec r/3$: the repaired estimator returns $\mathcal{M}(\rho)$, biased by a factor 3. Unbiasedness lives in the unphysical snapshot. If a physical estimate is needed, project the final average, not the individual records.

sections.heading: Many qubits: the price of a Pauli string

blocks.md: With independent random bases on every qubit, $U = U_1\otimes\cdots\otimes U_n$ and the outcome is a product $|b\rangle = |b_1\rangle\otimes\cdots\otimes|b_n\rangle$. The channel factorizes, so its inverse does too, and the snapshot is a tensor product of single-qubit snapshots [@shadows]:

Take a Pauli string $P = P_1\otimes\cdots\otimes P_n$ with support $S$ (the qubits where $P_j \ne I$) and weight $k = |S|$. Since $\operatorname{Tr}(\hat\rho_j) = 1$ off the support and $\operatorname{Tr}(P_j\hat\rho_j) = 3\,b_j$ if qubit $j$ was measured in basis $P_j$ and $0$ otherwise (because $\operatorname{Tr}\big(P_j\,\tfrac12(I + 3bQ)\big) = 0$ when $Q \ne P_j$),

blocks.title: Exact cost of a Pauli string
blocks.label: prop-l7-07-variance
blocks.md: For random Pauli shadows and a Pauli string $P$ of weight $k$, for every state $\rho$: $\mathbb{E}[\hat o_P] = \langle P\rangle$ and $\mathbb{E}[\hat o_P^2] = 3^k$, so $\operatorname{Var}\hat o_P = 3^k - \langle P\rangle^2$. The mean of $N$ independent snapshots has standard error $\sqrt{(3^k - \langle P\rangle^2)/N}$.

By [](#eq-l7-07-estimator), $\hat o_P = 0$ unless all $k$ bases on the support match, an event of probability $3^{-k}$ that does not depend on $\rho$, because bases are chosen before the measurement. On that event $\hat o_P = 3^k\prod_{j\in S} b_j$ with $b_j = \pm 1$, so $\hat o_P^2 = 9^k$ and $\mathbb{E}[\hat o_P^2] = 3^{-k}\cdot 9^k = 3^k$. Given that all bases match, the qubits in $S$ were measured in the eigenbases of the $P_j$, and the product of the eigenvalues $\prod_j b_j$ has expectation $\operatorname{Tr}(P\rho)$. Hence $\mathbb{E}[\hat o_P] = 3^{-k}\cdot 3^k\langle P\rangle = \langle P\rangle$. The variance and the standard error of a mean of independent copies follow.

blocks.alt: A grid of 12 shots by 4 qubits with random letters X, Y, Z; rows whose bases match a target Pauli string are boxed and score 3, 9 or nothing, followed by the variance formula.
blocks.caption: A weight-$k$ Pauli string only uses the shots whose $k$ bases all match. As $k$ grows the hits become rare and large: $\Pr = 3^{-k}$, value $\pm 3^k$.
blocks.describe: Twelve seeded shots on four qubits are listed with their random bases. The state is $|{+}\rangle|0\rangle|{+}i\rangle|0\rangle$, so every target below has true value 1. For $P = X\otimes I\otimes I\otimes I$ ($k = 1$), the 5 shots that measured qubit 1 in $X$ are boxed and each scores 3: mean $5\cdot 3/12 = 1.25$. For $X\otimes Z\otimes I\otimes I$ ($k = 2$) only 2 shots match and each scores 9: mean $2\cdot 9/12 = 1.5$. For $X\otimes Z\otimes Y\otimes Z$ ($k = 4$) no shot matches and the estimate is 0. The rules appear: the probability that all $k$ bases match is $3^{-k}$, $\hat o_P \in \{0, \pm 3^k\}$, $\mathbb{E}[\hat o_P^2] = 3^{-k}\cdot 9^k = 3^k$, and $\operatorname{Var}\hat o_P = 3^k - \langle P\rangle^2$. The last line notes that for $k = 50$, $3^{50} \approx 7.2\times 10^{23}$.

blocks.title: Pauli strings, tensor products and general local observables
blocks.label: rem-l7-07-local
blocks.md: For a general observable $O$ acting on at most $k$ qubits, Huang, Kueng and Preskill prove $\|O - \tfrac{\operatorname{Tr} O}{2^n} I\|_{\mathrm{shadow}}^2 \le 4^{k}\|O\|_\infty^2$ for random Pauli measurements, and note that the scaling improves to $3^k$ when $O$ is a tensor product of $k$ single-qubit observables [@shadows]. [](#prop-l7-07-variance) is the exact statement for Pauli strings. A sum of many local terms (a Hamiltonian, say) is not itself a weight-$k$ string; its variance includes covariances between terms, so estimate the terms and add them, or bound the sum separately.

sections.heading: The shadow norm and the Huang-Kueng-Preskill guarantee

blocks.title: Shadow norm
blocks.label: def-l7-07-norm
blocks.md: For a measurement primitive $\mathcal{U}$ with channel $\mathcal{M}$, $\|O\|_{\mathrm{shadow}} = \max_{\sigma\ \text{state}} \Big(\mathbb{E}_{U\sim\mathcal{U}} \sum_{b\in\{0,1\}^n} \langle b|U\sigma U^\dagger|b\rangle\, \langle b|U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)U^\dagger|b\rangle^2\Big)^{1/2}$. It depends only on the ensemble, not on the unknown state [@shadows]. Because $\mathcal{M}^{-1}$ is self-adjoint, $\langle b|U\mathcal{M}^{-1}(O)U^\dagger|b\rangle = \operatorname{Tr}(O\hat\rho)$ for the snapshot of outcome $b$, so the bracket is the second moment $\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\hat o^2]$ when the state is $\sigma$. For a Pauli string of weight $k$ under random Pauli measurements, [](#prop-l7-07-variance) gives $\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\hat o_P^2] = 3^k$ for every $\sigma$, hence $\|P\|_{\mathrm{shadow}}^2 = 3^k$ exactly.

blocks.title: Variance of one snapshot (Huang, Kueng and Preskill, Lemma 1)
blocks.label: lem-l7-07-var
blocks.md: For $\hat o = \operatorname{Tr}(O\hat\rho)$ with $\hat\rho$ a snapshot, $\operatorname{Var}[\hat o] \le \big\|O - \tfrac{\operatorname{Tr}(O)}{2^n} I\big\|_{\mathrm{shadow}}^2$. Subtracting the trace part costs nothing, because every snapshot has unit trace.

blocks.title: Median-of-means prediction with classical shadows (Huang, Kueng and Preskill, Theorem 1)
blocks.label: thm-l7-07-hkp
blocks.md: Fix a measurement primitive $\mathcal{U}$, Hermitian $2^n\times 2^n$ matrices $O_1, \dots, O_M$ and accuracy parameters $\epsilon, \delta \in [0, 1]$. Set $K = 2\log(2M/\delta)$ and $N = \dfrac{34}{\epsilon^2}\max_{1\le i\le M} \big\|O_i - \tfrac{\operatorname{Tr}(O_i)}{2^n} I\big\|_{\mathrm{shadow}}^2$. Then $NK$ independent snapshots, split into $K$ groups of $N$, give median-of-means estimates $\hat o_i(N, K)$ (the median of the $K$ group means of $\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\hat\rho)$) with $|\hat o_i(N, K) - \operatorname{Tr}(O_i\rho)| \le \epsilon$ for all $1 \le i \le M$, with probability at least $1 - \delta$ [@shadows].

blocks.title: How to read the constants
blocks.label: rem-l7-07-constants
blocks.md: The logarithm is natural: the proof bounds each median's failure probability by $2e^{-K/2}$ and asks for $\delta/M$, which gives $K = 2\ln(2M/\delta)$. The authors state that the constants come from a conservative worst-case argument and expect the actual constants to be much smaller in practice [@shadows]. What the theorem does buy is the shape: the number of observables enters only through $\ln M$, the number of qubits does not enter explicitly, and everything else sits in one norm. The observables may be chosen after the data are collected. The theorem counts snapshots only; the classical cost of evaluating $\operatorname{Tr}(O_i\hat\rho_j)$ is extra and is cheap for Pauli strings because of [](#eq-l7-07-estimator).

blocks.title: A self-contained median-of-means bound
blocks.label: lem-l7-07-mom
blocks.md: Let $X$ have variance at most $\sigma^2$. Split $NK$ independent copies into $K$ groups of size $N \ge 4\sigma^2/\epsilon^2$ and let $\hat\mu$ be the median of the group means.
