blocks.caption: The six open problems and the lessons whose tools they use.

sections.heading: From open problem to research question

blocks.md: A research question is an open problem cut down to a size that one study can answer, with a comparison that can fail. The original direction is rarely the question: "is quantum causal discovery more efficient?" has no truth value until the model class, access, accuracy and baseline are fixed.

blocks.title: Adaptive designs for channel discrimination
blocks.label: ex-l7-10-adaptive
blocks.md: Direction: adaptive experiment selection for quantum causal discovery. Question: for discriminating a direct cause from a common cause in the two-qubit classes of [L7-05](#lesson-l7-05), does choosing the next Pauli basis adaptively reduce the shots needed for error at most $\delta$, compared with the best fixed allocation at equal total shots? Assumptions: trusted measurement calibration; true triples at distance at least $\eta$ from the octahedron. Falsifier: equal or higher error at equal shots, or a gain that disappears under calibration drift, which would be reported as the boundary of the method. A general causal advantage is not claimed from this restricted result.

blocks.title: A boundary is a contribution
blocks.md: Showing exactly where a method stops working (a noise level, a model class, a cost left out of an earlier comparison) is a result. Many of the known entries in the atlas above are of this kind: barren plateaus bound trainability, dequantization bounds speed-ups, and the fact that the switch violates no causal inequality [@process] marks what a causal-inequality test cannot detect.

worked_example.title: Auditing a hypothetical claim to its supported form
worked_example.problem: Audit the hypothetical sentence "Our quantum causal learner tells cause from common cause with perfect accuracy: an exponential advantage", using the two-qubit Pauli-correlation test as the method actually run.
steps: Type signature. Task: decide common cause versus direct cause. Model class: shared two-qubit states, and channels with a maximally mixed, measured and re-prepared input (L7-05). Access: projective $XX$, $YY$, $ZZ$ measurements, $N$ shots each. Method: classify by the position of the estimated triple relative to $T_{cc}$, $T_{dc}$ and the octahedron. Baseline: classical observational data, which do not identify the direction at all. Evidence: a theorem for exact data, simulation for finite $N$.

Accuracy with exact data: by [](#prop-l7-10-half), the structure is determined for exactly half of each class by volume (the Monte Carlo check gives 0.502 of 4000), and is undetermined, not wrong, for the other half. "Perfect accuracy" is false; "never wrong with exact data" is true.

Finite shots (numerical evidence, stated prior): identified 0.339, undetermined 0.573, wrong 0.088 at $N = 25$; identified 0.399, wrong 0.044 at $N = 100$; identified 0.472, wrong 0.015 at $N = 1600$.

Advantage: there is no cost comparison at all; the quantum data identify something classical observational data cannot. "Exponential advantage" has no referent, and the quantifier check of [](#eq-l7-10-claim) fails at the first step.
worked_example.result: Supported sentence: for two qubits in the stated model classes, exact Pauli correlations determine the causal structure outside the octahedron, half of each class by volume, and a plug-in rule with $N$ shots per basis errs on a fraction that decreases with $N$ in simulation; this is an identifiability difference, not a speed-up.

exercises.prompt: A paper reports that its quantum model beats a classical neural network on three datasets. Fill in the type signature of [](#def-l7-10-claim) as far as this sentence allows, mark the missing slots, and say which evidence type it is.
exercises.solution: Task: the three prediction tasks; model class: the three data distributions only; access: unstated (how the data are loaded into the circuit, how many shots); accuracy and failure probability: unstated or as reported test error without uncertainty; method: the quantum model; resource bound: unstated; baseline: one classical network, not the best classical method with equal access; evidence: numerical (or hardware) evidence of an existential kind, $\exists$ instances where $A$ beats one $B$. It establishes neither an upper bound over a class nor a lower bound against all classical methods.

exercises.prompt: For the noisy family $P_v$, decide what the cut inflation says at $v = 0.6$ and at $v = 0.4$.
exercises.solution: At $v = 0.6$: the disagreement budget is $1 - v = 0.4 < 1/2$, so by [](#prop-l7-10-noisy) no $Q$ meets the constraints and $P_{0.6}$ is incompatible with the classical triangle. At $v = 0.4$: $1 - v = 0.6 \ge 1/2$, the constraints can be met (with $r = 0.1$ in the construction), and the cut inflation is silent: it neither proves nor disproves compatibility.

exercises.prompt: Verify the construction in the proof of [](#prop-l7-10-noisy) for $v = 0.3$: compute $r$ and $P(A_2 \ne B_1)$, and check that the pair $(A_2, B_1)$ has the table of $P_{0.3}$.
exercises.solution: $r = 1/2 - 0.3 = 0.2$. Before the flip, $P(A_2 \ne B_1) = P(A_2 \ne C_1) \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac14$. After flipping with probability $r$: $\tfrac14(1 - 0.2) + \tfrac34(0.2) = 0.2 + 0.15 = 0.35 = (1 - 0.3)/2$. By the global flip symmetry, $P(01) = P(10) = 0.175$ and $P(00) = P(11) = 0.325$, which is the $(A, B)$ table of $P_{0.3}$: $P(a = b) = 0.3 + 0.7/2 = 0.65$, split equally.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite the sentence "Quantum inflation solves quantum causal compatibility" so that it is accurate for the works described in this lesson.
exercises.solution: For example: "Quantum inflation gives a hierarchy of tests that can falsify compatibility of correlations with a quantum causal network; a modified version of the hierarchy is known to converge when local subsystems are modeled as commuting observable algebras, while completeness of the original hierarchy is, to our knowledge, open." The classical statement (the classical hierarchy converges) should not be transferred to the quantum case.

exercises.prompt: Prove that the octahedron $|c_1| + |c_2| + |c_3| \le 1$ equals $T_{cc} \cap T_{dc}$, using the facet inequalities $1 - s_1 c_1 - s_2 c_2 - s_3 c_3 \ge 0$, where $T_{cc}$ uses the sign patterns $(1,1,1)$, $(1,-1,-1)$, $(-1,1,-1)$ and $(-1,-1,1)$ for $s$, and $T_{dc}$ the negated patterns.
exercises.solution: Together the two tetrahedra impose $1 - s\cdot c \ge 0$ for all eight sign vectors $s \in \{\pm1\}^3$ (the four patterns with product $+1$ and their negatives, product $-1$). Maximizing $s \cdot c$ over all eight sign vectors gives $\sum_i |c_i|$ (choose $s_i = \operatorname{sign} c_i$). So $c$ lies in both tetrahedra exactly when $\sum_i |c_i| \le 1$.

exercises.prompt: Choose one open problem from the atlas and write a research question with: the model class, the access, one identifying assumption, the baseline, the evidence type you aim for, and one result that would count against your proposed method.
exercises.solution: Sample answer (problem 1): For two-qubit processes that are probabilistic mixtures of one shared state and one channel from the classes of L7-05, with only Pauli measurements and $N$ shots per basis, can the mixing weight be identified and estimated? Assumption: the mixture components lie outside the octahedron and measurements are calibrated. Baseline: the plug-in classifier of this lesson applied to the pure components. Evidence: an identifiability theorem plus a finite-sample bound, checked by a simulation protocol written in advance (L7-09). Counter-result: two different (weight, component) pairs that produce the same correlation triple, which would show the weight is not identified. Any answer is acceptable that fixes every slot and names a falsifying observation.

check.question: Which statement belongs in a research conclusion?
options: A universal advantage inferred from one toy simulation
A measured or proved result together with its model class and access limits
An open question presented as an established theorem
A speed-up stated without the baseline it was compared with
check.explanation: A defensible conclusion matches the scope of the evidence: the model assumptions and access limits determine where the proved or measured result applies.

check.question: For the noisy family $P_v$, the cut-inflation constraints can be met at $v = 0.4$. What does this show?
options: That $P_{0.4}$ is incompatible with the triangle
That quantum sources are needed for $P_{0.4}$
That $P_{0.4}$ is compatible with the triangle
Nothing about compatibility: the cut inflation is only a necessary condition
check.explanation: [](#lem-l7-10-cut) gives conditions every compatible distribution satisfies. Passing them does not prove compatibility; only failing them (for $v > 1/2$) gives a conclusion.

check.question: A simulation shows method $A$ uses fewer shots than baseline $B$ on 20 random instances of size up to 12. What would a separation additionally require?
options: A hardware run of $A$ on the same instances
An upper bound for $A$ on all instances of each size and a lower bound against every competing method with the same access
More random instances of the same sizes
A larger number of shots for $B$
check.explanation: The simulation is existential evidence against one baseline. A separation needs the two universal statements of [](#eq-l7-10-claim) and the lower bound beside it; more instances or hardware runs do not change the quantifiers.

check.question: In the quantum switch of two unitaries $A$ and $B$ with control $|+\rangle$, what happens to the control when $AB = -BA$?
options: It is maximally mixed
It depends on the target state
It ends in $|+\rangle$ with certainty
It ends in $|-\rangle$ with certainty
check.explanation: The output is $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle BA|\psi\rangle + |1\rangle AB|\psi\rangle) = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(|0\rangle - |1\rangle) \otimes BA|\psi\rangle$ when $AB = -BA$, so the control is $|-\rangle$ for every target, as the code in this lesson confirms.

misconceptions.claim: "Many simulations on random instances amount to a proof of advantage."
misconceptions.correction: Simulations give existential evidence against particular baselines. An advantage needs an upper bound for the method over a class and a lower bound against every competitor with the same access; no number of instances supplies the second.

misconceptions.claim: "Inflation decides causal compatibility."
misconceptions.correction: Each inflation gives necessary conditions; passing a level proves nothing. For classical sources the full hierarchy converges (Navascues and Wolfe); for the original quantum hierarchy completeness is described as open, and the known convergent quantum version is a modified hierarchy in a commuting-operator setting.

misconceptions.claim: "Experiments with the quantum switch have shown that nature has indefinite causal order, full stop."
misconceptions.correction: Photonic switch experiments [@procopio] and a witness-based verification of causal nonseparability [@rubino] rest on assumptions about the devices, and the switch violates no causal inequality [@process]; what such data show about causal order depends on those stated assumptions.

misconceptions.claim: "An open problem in a survey is the same as a research question."
misconceptions.correction: A research question fixes model class, access, accuracy, baseline and a falsifying result, so that one study can answer it; an open problem is usually a family of such questions.

lessons.connect: This lesson closes Level 7 and the course. It reuses identifiability ([L7-05](#lesson-l7-05)), resource accounting ([L7-06](#lesson-l7-06)), protocols ([L7-09](#lesson-l7-09)), process matrices ([L6-07](#lesson-l6-07)) and the quantum switch ([L6-08](#lesson-l6-08)). The natural next step is a research project: pick one atlas entry, write the protocol of L7-09 for a question cut from it, and audit your own draft claim before anyone else does.
lessons.caution: The atlas is a research-entry synthesis, not an exhaustive survey, and the field moves quickly: verify the current literature before claiming novelty or the current state of the art. "Open" means open in the cited sources as of writing; the "solved when" criteria are this lesson's proposals, not field consensus. The statements about inflation hierarchies, the barren-plateau and simulability perspective, and dequantization go no further than the cited works state; the perspective in particular argues from examples, not from a general theorem. The audit's finite-shot rates are simulations under a uniform prior on correlation triples, which is a modeling choice; the perfect-correlation argument is proved here for classical sources only.

instructor.why: Doctoral and postdoctoral students must judge claims faster than they can reproduce them. Giving every claim a type signature, separating existential from universal evidence, and stating open problems with criteria for solution makes critical reading teachable [@inflation; @advantage; @plateaus; @process].
teaching_notes: Run the audit live on a recent abstract chosen by the students; fill the type signature on the board and mark empty slots before reading the body of the paper.
Do the cut-inflation proof by hand before showing the animation; ask students to guess the threshold for the noisy family first.
Assign each student one atlas entry to update from the current literature, with every new claim placed in a type signature and given an evidence type.
Stress the difference between "undetermined" and "wrong" in the audit: an identification failure is not an error rate.
instructor.assessment: The challenge exercise asking for a research question from the atlas is the main assessment, graded on whether every slot is fixed and the falsifier is concrete; the stretch exercise on rewriting the quantum inflation sentence tests faithful attribution.
instructor.extend: Read the inflation paper's proof that the W-type distribution is incompatible with the triangle [@inflation] and compare it with the cut-inflation argument here: which inflation does it need, and why does the cut inflation not suffice? Then write the linear program for that inflation.

further.note: Causal inference for a bipartite system at two times from light-touch coarse-grained measurements.
Experimental verification of causal nonseparability of a quantum switch with a causal witness.
A framework of quantum causal models in which latent quantum systems can be nodes.
Noise-induced barren plateaus, a second route to untrainability.

unit.big_question: When does a quantum learning method answer a causal question better than the alternatives, and what evidence, identification argument and resource count would establish it?
unit.summary: The unit treats Quantum Causal AI as a set of research questions, not a finished method. Learners first separate prediction, causal identification and quantum resource claims, then study the two workhorses of quantum learning, variational circuits with parameter-shift gradients and quantum kernels, with exact derivations and complete shot accounting. They analyze trainability and barren plateaus, prove identifiability before learning, and build resource ledgers that keep copies, queries, gates and time apart. Classical shadows show how observable structure controls estimation cost. The unit ends with reproducible benchmark design, a falsifiable research protocol with stopping rules, and a critical synthesis of open problems.
unit.for_whom: Doctoral students and postdoctoral researchers in physics, computer science, statistics or a quantitative field who have completed Levels 4 to 6 or know structural causal models, density operators and channels, and quantum causal models. Each lesson works as a seminar session, a reading-group module or self-study.
unit.prerequisites: Structural causal models and identification (Level 4), quantum states, channels and measurements (Level 5), quantum causal models and process descriptions (Level 6), and fluency with linear algebra, probability and Python with numpy.

time.pace: One lesson a week with the project running alongside fits a twelve-week seminar: ten lesson weeks and two project weeks. Each lesson splits into a derivation session (animations, theorems, proofs) and a computation session (code, interactive figures, exercises).

session_flow: Before the session: read the motivation and attempt the review check from memory.
Watch the animations and reconstruct each derivation on paper before reading the proof.
Run the code blocks, change one parameter, and predict the output before running it again.
Work the worked example, then one core, one stretch and one challenge exercise.
Discuss: classify a recent paper's claims with the lesson's tools and write a short referee note.
Instructors: use the teaching notes and the assessment suggestion at the end of each lesson.

outcomes.text: Specify a research task by its data access, target, model class, error criterion and budget, and separate prediction, causal and resource claims.
Derive the parameter-shift rule from the spectrum of the generator and compare its bias, variance and circuit cost with finite differences under shot noise.
Evaluate a quantum kernel claim with its full cost: positive semidefiniteness, shots per Gram entry, concentration, and the geometric difference to classical kernels.
Distinguish vanishing true gradients from noisy estimates and design a controlled trainability study across system sizes.
Prove or disprove identifiability of a target under a stated data map and model class before fitting a flexible model.
Keep copies, queries, gates and wall-clock time apart in a resource ledger, and explain how observable structure controls classical-shadow cost.
Design a reproducible benchmark and a falsifiable protocol with stopping rules that separate prediction from causal recovery.
Formulate an open research question with its evidence requirements, without presenting a proposal as a result.

unit.evidence: Each lesson ends with four check questions, one reviewing an earlier lesson, and exercises at core, stretch and challenge levels with complete solutions. Several challenge exercises are written as referee reports on a described paper. The capstone is a pre-registered research protocol with a reproducible simulation study, judged with a four-part rubric.
materials: Python 3 with numpy, scipy, matplotlib and plotly (the course package qcai for the lab notebooks)
A Jupyter environment (local, Colab or Binder) for the lessons' code and the labs
Access to the cited papers (all have open arXiv versions)
Optional: a quantum software framework such as PennyLane for comparison with the hand-written simulators
Optional: access to a cloud quantum device, with its calibration data recorded

project.title: A pre-registered quantum causal learning study
project.summary: Over four sessions the learner turns a research question into a specified task, proves or disproves identification of its target, writes a protocol with resource budget and stopping rules, runs a reproducible simulation study against strong classical baselines, and reports results with the limits of what they show.
questions: Can a variational or kernel model recover the effect of an intervention on a simulated quantum process better than a classical learner given the same measurement records, and what identifies that effect?
For a family of feature maps, how does the geometric difference to tuned classical kernels scale with qubits, and at what shot budget do Gram matrix estimates stop being informative?
Under a fixed shot budget, which gradient estimator and initialization strategy keeps a variational circuit trainable as it grows, and how would you tell a barren plateau from estimation noise?
steps: Write the task specification: data access, target formula, model class, error criterion and resource budget.
Prove identification of the target under the stated access, or construct two data-equivalent models that disprove it and revise the design.
Pre-register the protocol: hypotheses, metrics, classical baselines, system sizes, seeds, shot budgets and stopping rules.
Implement the simulation with fixed seeds, unit tests against closed forms, and a complete resource ledger.
Run the study across sizes, report uncertainty for every metric, and compare with the tuned baselines.
Write the report: claims matched to evidence, limits, and what result would have falsified the hypothesis.

rubric.start: The task is described in words and the target is implicit.
rubric.got: The target is a formula, and identification is argued under stated assumptions.
rubric.explain: Identification is proved, or disproved by a constructed counterexample, and the design is adjusted accordingly.

rubric.start: Some costs are reported, such as circuit depth.
rubric.got: Shots, circuit settings, data loading and classical post-processing are counted.
rubric.explain: Costs are given as functions of size and accuracy, and the comparison fixes the access model for all methods.

rubric.start: One classical method is run with default settings.
rubric.got: Tuned classical baselines and uncertainty intervals are reported for every metric.
rubric.explain: Baselines are chosen to be the strongest available for the access model, and conclusions survive the uncertainty.

rubric.start: Code runs, but seeds and settings are incomplete.
rubric.got: Seeds, versions, protocol and stopping rules are fixed in advance and reported.
rubric.explain: Every claim is matched to its evidence, limits are explicit, and a falsifying outcome is stated.

udl: Every derivation appears three ways: as an animation with a full text description, as a theorem with proof, and as runnable code.
Interactive figures let learners vary one parameter at a time, and each comes with a written description of what changes.
Learners can show mastery through proofs, code, written referee reports or an oral presentation of the project.
Exercises are tiered core, stretch and challenge, so a seminar can assign different depths to different participants.

readings.note: A survey of quantum machine learning task classes and the access assumptions behind them.
Review of variational quantum algorithms, their training and their limitations.
Conditions under which parameter-shift rules give exact gradients on hardware.
The power-of-data analysis: when classical learners with data match quantum models.
Gradient concentration in random parametrized circuits.
Process-based quantum causal modelling, the framework for causal questions about quantum systems.
Causal AI from structural causal models through identification and learning.
Classical shadows and how observable structure controls estimation cost.

unit.approach: The unit is planned backward from research outcomes [@ubd_whitepaper]: each lesson moves from a motivating failure to a precise statement, a proof or proof sketch, computation, and practice [@merrill2002], with a review question in every check for spaced retrieval [@dunlosky2013]. Animations are made with Manim Community Edition [@manim_ce] from the same numbers the text states, and every lesson offers several ways to engage and to show understanding [@udl]. The quantum learning content follows the primary literature on variational algorithms and gradients [@vqa; @mitarai; @schuld], kernels and the power of data [@kernels; @advantage], and trainability [@plateaus; @noise]; the causal content follows Pearl and Bareinboim [@pearlcausality; @bareinboim] and process-based quantum causal modelling [@costa]. Claims of quantum advantage are always paired with resource accounting and classical baselines.
